INTRODUCTION

Much has been written about the chronology of Alexandrian literature and the famous Library, founded by Ptolemy Soter, but the dates of the chief writers are still matters of conjecture. The birth of Apollonius Rhodius is placed by scholars at various times between 296 and 260 BC, while the year of his death is equally uncertain. In fact, we have very little information on the subject. There are two "lives" of Apollonius in the Scholia, both derived from an earlier one which is lost. From these we learn that he was of Alexandria by birth,¹ that he lived in the time of the Ptolemies, and was a pupil of Callimachus; that while still a youth he composed and recited in public his Argonautica, and that the poem was condemned, as a result of which he retired to Rhodes; that there he revised his

¹ "Or of Naucratis," according to Aelian and Athenaeus.

INTRODUCTION

poem, recited it with great applause, and hence called himself a Rhodian. The second "life" adds: "Some say that he returned to Alexandria and again recited his poem with the utmost success, so that he was honoured with the libraries of the Museum¹ and was buried with Callimachus." The last sentence may be interpreted in light of the notice of Suidas, who informs us that Apollonius was a contemporary of Eratosthenes, Euphorion, and Timarchus, in the time of Ptolemy Euergetes, and that he succeeded Eratosthenes as head of the Alexandrian Library. Suidas also informs us elsewhere that Aristophanes, at the age of sixty-two, succeeded Apollonius in this office. Many modern scholars deny the "bibliothecariate" of Apollonius for chronological reasons, and there is considerable difficulty about it. The date of Callimachus' Hymn to Apollo, which closes with some lines (105–113) that are admittedly an allusion to Apollonius, may be placed with much probability at 248 or 247 B.C. Apollonius must at that date have been at least twenty years old. Eratosthenes died 196–193 B.C. This would make Apollonius seventy-two to seventy-five when he succeeded Eratosthenes. This is not impossible, it is true, but it is difficult. But the difficulty is

¹ "that he was deemed worthy of the libraries of the Museum."

vi

INTRODUCTION

passage at the end of the Hymn to Apollo, already mentioned, also probably in some epigrams, but most of all in his Ibis, of which we have an imitation, or perhaps nearly a translation, in Ovid's poem of the same name. On the part of Apollonius there is a passage in the third book of the Argonautica (lines 927–947) which is polemical in nature and stands out from its context, along with the well-known savage epigram aimed at Callimachus.1 Various explanations have been attempted by scholars, notably by Couat in his Poésie Alexandrine, to give a coherent account of the quarrel, but we do not have sufficient evidence to determine the order of the attacks, replies, and counter-attacks. The Ibis has been thought to mark the end of the feud, on the curious grounds that the abuse had nowhere further to go. It was an age when literary men were more inclined to comment on the writings of the past than to produce original work. Literature was engaged in taking stock of itself. Homer was, of course, universally admired, but more admired than imitated. Epic poetry was out of fashion, and we find many epigrams of this period—some by Callimachus—directed against the "cyclic" poets, by whom were meant at that time those who were always dragging in con-

It constitutes a metrical guidebook, filled no doubt with many pleasing episodes, such as the abduction of Hylas, the boxing match between Pollux and Amycus, the account of Cyzicus, the account of the Amazons, and the legend of Talos — but there is no unity running through the poem beyond that of the voyage itself.

The Tale of the Argonauts had been told many times before, in both verse and prose, and the names of many authors are given in the Scholia to Apollonius, but their works have not survived. The best-known earlier account we have is that in Pindar's fourth Pythian Ode, from which Apollonius drew many details. The subject was well suited to an epic poem, since its unity might have been found in the working out of the expiation owed for the crime of Athamas; but this motive is barely mentioned by our author.

As we have it, the motive for the voyage is the command of Pelias to bring back the golden fleece, and this command is rooted in Pelias' desire to destroy Jason, while the divine aid given to Jason stems from Hera's intention to punish Pelias for his neglect of the honor due to her. The learning of Apollonius is not deep, but it is curious; his general sentiments are not in keeping with Alexandrian standards, for they are simple and obvious. In the mass of material from which he had to choose

INTRODUCTION

useful bridge between Athens and Rome. The Argonautica was translated by Varro Atacinus, copied by Ovid and Virgil, and minutely studied by Valerius Flaccus in his poem of the same name. Some of his finest passages have been appropriated and improved upon by Virgil by the divine right of superior genius.1 The subject of love had been treated in the romantic spirit before the time of Apollonius in writings that have perished, for instance, in those of Antimachus of Colophon, but the Argonautica is perhaps the first poem still extant in which the expression of this spirit is developed with elaboration. The Medea of Apollonius is the direct precursor of the Dido of Virgil, and it is the pathos and passion of the fourth book of the Aeneid that keep alive many a passage of Apollonius.

1 e.g. compare Aen. iv. 305 ff. with Ap. Rh. iv. 355 ff., Aen. iv. 327–330 with Ap. Rh. i. 897, 898, Aen. iv. 522 ff., with Ap. Rh. iii. 744 ff.

BIBLIOGRAPHY.

Two editions of the Argonautica were published by Apollonius. Of these we have only the second. The Scholia preserve a few passages of the first edition, from which the second seems to have differed only slightly. The old opinion that our manuscripts preserve any traces of the first edition has long been given up. The principal manuscripts are the following:—

The Laurentian, also called the Medicean, XXXII. 9, of the early eleventh century, is the excellent manuscript at Florence which contains Sophocles, Aeschylus, and Apollonius Rhodius. This is by far the best authority for the text (here denoted by L).
The Guelferbytanus of the thirteenth century closely agrees with another Laurentian, XXXII. 16, of the same date (here denoted by G and L² respectively).

In the early eleventh century there were two types of text: the first is best known to us through L, the second through G and L² and the corrections made in L. Quotations in the Etymologicum Magnum agree with the second type and show that it is as old as the fifth century. Besides these there are, of inferior quality, four Vatican manuscripts and five Parisian ones, which are occasionally useful. Most of them have Scholia; the best Scholia are those of L.

The principal editions are:—

Florence, 1496, quarto. This is the editio princeps, by Lascaris, based on L, with Scholia — a very rare book.
Venice, 1521, octavo. The Aldine, by Franciscus Asulanus, with Scholia.
Paris, 1541, octavo, based on the Parisian manuscripts.
Geneva, 1574, quarto, by Stephanus, with Scholia.
Leyden, 1641, 2 vols., octavo, by J. Hölzlin, with a Latin translation.
Oxford, 1777, 2 vols., quarto, by J. Shaw, with a Latin translation.
Strassburg, 1780, octavo and quarto, by R. F. P. Brunck.

Rome, 1791–1794, 2 vols., 4to, by Flangini, with an Italian translation.
Leipzig, 1797, 8vo, by Ch. D. Beck, with a Latin version. A second volume, intended to contain the Scholia and a commentary, was never published.
Leipzig, 1810–1813, 2 vols., 8vo. A second edition of Brunck by G. H. Schäfer, with the Florentine and Parisian Scholia, the latter printed for the first time.
Leipzig, 1828, 8vo, by A. Wellauer, with the Scholia, both Florentine and Parisian.
Paris, 1841, 4to, by F. S. Lehrs, with a Latin version. In the Didot series.
Leipzig, 1852, 8vo, by R. Merkel, "based on the Laurentian manuscript." The Teubner Text.
Leipzig, 1854, 2 vols., 8vo, by R. Merkel. The second volume contains Merkel's prolegomena and the Scholia to L, edited by H. Keil.
Oxford, 1900, 8vo, by R. C. Seaton. In the "Scriptorum Classicorum Bibliotheca Oxoniensis" series.

The text of the present edition is, with a few exceptions, that of the Oxford edition prepared by me for the Delegates of the Clarendon Press, whom I hereby thank for their permission to use it.

The English translations of Apollonius are as follows:—

By E. B. Greene, by F. Fawkes, both 1780; by W. Preston, 1803. None of these are of value. There is a prose translation by E. P. Coleridge in the Bohn Series. The most recent and also the best is a verse translation by Mr. A. S. Way, 1901, in "The Temple Classics."
I may also mention the excellent translation into French by Prof. H. de La Ville de Mirmont of the University of Bordeaux, 1892.

For Alexandrian literature in general, Couat's Poésie Alexandrine sous les trois premiers Ptolemées, 1882, may be recommended. Susemihl's Geschichte der Griechischen Litteratur in der Alexandinerzeit, 2 vols., 1891, is a perfect storehouse of facts and authorities, but is better suited for reference than for general reading. Morris' Life and Death of Jason is a poem that in many passages singularly resembles Apollonius in its pessimistic tone and spirit.

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS
THE ARGONAUTICA

BOOK I

APOLLONIUS OF RHODES
ARGONAUTICA

Book I

Beginning with you, Phoebus, I will recount the famous deeds of men of old, who sailed through the mouth of the Black Sea and between the Clashing Rocks, by command of King Pelias, to win the golden fleece aboard the well-benched Argo.
    For Pelias had heard an oracle that a grim fate awaited him at the hands of whatever man he should see coming from the people wearing only one sandal, and that he would be destroyed by that man's scheming. Not long after, in accordance with the true prophecy, Jason, crossing the winter-swollen waters of the Anaurus on foot, saved one sandal from the mud but left the other caught in the current at the ford. He came straightway to Pelias, to attend a feast which Pelias was celebrating for his father Poseidon and the other gods, though he paid no heed to Hera of Pelasgia. Pelias took one look at Jason and recognized him at once, and devised for him the toil of a perilous sea-voyage, so that either on the deep or among foreign peoples Jason might lose his homecoming.

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

THE ARGONAUTICA

BOOK I

Beginning with you, O Phoebus, I will recount the famous deeds of men of old, who, at the command of King Pelias, sailed through the mouth of the Black Sea and between the Clashing Rocks, driving the well-oared Argo in search of the golden fleece.
This was the oracle Pelias had heard: that a hateful doom awaited him—to be killed at the instigation of the man he would see coming from the people wearing only one sandal. Not long after, in fulfillment of that true prophecy, Jason crossed the wintry stream of Anaurus on foot, and rescued one sandal from the mud, but left the other held fast in the depths by the flood. He went straight to Pelias to share in the feast the king was offering to his father Poseidon and the other gods, though he paid no honor to Hera of Pelasgia. The king saw him at once, took note, and devised for him the hardship of a dangerous voyage, so that Jason might lose his homecoming on the sea or among strangers.

Now the ship, which the bards of old celebrate as built by Argus under the guidance of Athena — let me now tell of the lineage and names of the heroes, and their long voyage over the sea, and all they accomplished in their wandering. May the Muses be the inspirers of my song.

Let us first remember Orpheus, whom Calliope herself is said to have borne to Thracian Oeagrus, near the heights of Pimpleia. Men say that he once charmed with his singing the unyielding rocks on the mountains and the rushing rivers. As tokens of that song, the wild oaks still stand on the Thracian shore at Zone, growing in close rows along the coast — those he led down from Pieria, enchanting them with his lyre. Such was the Orpheus whom Aeson's son, trusting the advice of Chiron, welcomed as a helper in his toils — Orpheus, who ruled over Bistonian Pieria.

Then came Asterion, born near the swirling waters of the Apidanus to Cometes, who dwelt near Mount Phylleius at Peiresiae, where the great Apidanus and the noble Enipeus join together, flowing from afar into one stream.

After them, leaving Larisa, came Polyphemus, son of Eilatus, who in earlier days had fought among the mighty Lapiths when the Lapiths armed themselves against the Centaurs — though now his limbs were heavy with age, his warrior spirit remained as strong as ever.

Nor did Iphiclus long remain at Phylace — he was the maternal uncle of Aeson's son, for he had married his sister.

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK I

The ship, as earlier poets tell, was built by Argus under the guidance of Athena. But now I will recount the lineage and names of the heroes, their long sea-voyages, and the deeds they performed in their wanderings; may the Muses inspire my song!
Let us begin by naming Orpheus, whom Calliope, it is said, bore to the Thracian Oeagrus near the Pimpleian heights. Men say that by the music of his songs he charmed the stubborn rocks on the mountainsides and turned the course of rivers. And the wild oak-trees at Zone on the Thracian shore, tokens of that magical power, still stand in ordered rows to this day — the very trees he led down from Pieria by the spell of his lyre. Such was Orpheus, whom Aeson's son welcomed as a companion in his labors, at the command of Cheiron — Orpheus, ruler of Bistonian Pieria.
Next came Asterion, whom Cometes fathered by the swirling waters of the Apidanus; he lived at Peiresiae near the Phylleian mount, where the mighty Apidanus and the bright Enipeus flow together, joining their currents from afar.
After them came Polyphemus from Larisa, son of Eilatus, who in earlier days had fought among the great Lapithae when they took up arms against the Centaurs; his limbs were now heavy with age, but his warrior spirit remained as strong as ever.
Nor was Iphiclus slow to join them at Phylace — the uncle of Aeson's son, for Aeson had married his

Aison urged Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus, whom kinship and family bond moved him to include in the company.

Nor did Admetus, lord of Pherae with its fine flocks, remain beneath the watch-peak of the Chalcodonian mountain.

Nor did the sons of Hermes stay at Alope — those skilled in trickery, Erytus and Echion — and with them as a third came their kinsman Aethalides as they set out. The one of them was born by the Phthian daughter of Myrmidion, Eupolemeia, on the banks of the Amphryssus; but the other two were born of Antianeira, daughter of Menetes.

And Coronus, son of Caeneus, came, leaving wealthy Gyrton behind — a brave man, yet no better than his father. For the poets still celebrate how Caeneus, though still alive, perished among the Centaurs, when alone and apart from the other heroes he drove them off; and they, charging back against him, could neither beat him down nor slay him; but unbroken and unbending he sank beneath the earth, overwhelmed by the mighty fir-trees raining down upon him.

And there came also Mopsus of Titaresus, whom the son of Leto had taught beyond all others the divination of birds; and also Eurydamas, son of Ctimenus, who dwelt near lake Xynias, in Ctimene of the Dolopians.

And Actor roused his son Menoetius from Opus to go with the warrior men.

And there followed Eurytio and the mighty Eribotes — one the son of Teleon, the other the son of Irus, son of Actor; the glorious Eribotes was son of Teleon, and Eurytio of Irus. And with them as a third came Oileus, outstanding in valor and skilled at charging the enemy from behind whenever they break their ranks.

And from Euboea came Canthus, whom Canethus, son of Abas, sent eagerly; yet he was not destined —

The same text is already in English. Here it is rendered in clear, modern prose:

Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus, was Jason's sister, and his kinship with her ensured that he was counted among the crew. Nor did Admetus, lord of sheep-rich Pherae, remain behind beneath the peak of the Chalcodonian mountain. Nor did the sons of Hermes linger at Alope — men wealthy in farmland and highly skilled in cunning: Erytus and Echion. With them on their departure went their kinsman Aethalides as a third. Near the streams of Amphrysus, Eupolemeia, daughter of Myrmidon and from Phthia, had borne him; the other two were born of Antianeira, daughter of Menetes. From wealthy Gyrton came Coronus, son of Caeneus — brave, yet not braver than his father. Bards tell that Caeneus, though still living, perished at the hands of the Centaurs: apart from the other chiefs he had routed them, but when they rallied against him, they could neither bend him nor kill him; unconquered and unyielding, he passed down beneath the earth, overwhelmed by the crushing downfall of massive pine trees. There also came Titaresian Mopsus, whom the son of Leto had taught the reading of bird omens beyond all other men; and Eurydamas, son of Ctimenus, who lived at Dolopian Ctimene near the Xynian lake. Furthermore, Actor sent his son Menoetius from Opus to accompany the chiefs. Eurytion followed, and with him the mighty Eribotes — one the son of Teleon, the other of Irus, Actor's son: the renowned Eribotes, son of Teleon, and Eurytion, son of Irus. A third with them was Oileus, peerless in courage and highly skilled at pursuing a fleeing enemy when they break ranks. Then from Euboea came Canthus, eager for the quest, sent by Canethus son of Abas; yet he was —

...to return to Corinthus on his homeward way. For fate decreed that he and Mopsus, skilled in prophecy, should both perish wandering on the shores of Libya. Indeed it is no small evil that men reap, when even those two were buried in Libya, so far from Colchis as the distance between the setting and rising of the sun.

Next to join the company were Clytius and Iphitus, guardians of Oechalia, sons of stern Eurytus — that Eurytus to whom the Far-Shooter gave his bow, yet he gained no benefit from that gift, for of his own will he strove against the giver.

After these came the sons of Aeacus, yet not both together, nor from the same place — for they had settled apart, fleeing from Aegina, when in their folly they had slain their brother Phocus. Telamon had made his home on an island off Attica, while Peleus departed and dwelt in the halls of Phthia.

From Cecrops' city came the warrior Butes, son of noble Teleon, and with him the skilled spearman Phalerus. Alcon, his father, sent him forth — though he had no other sons to care for him in old age — yet, only child though he was, he sent him, that he might shine among the bold heroes.

As for Theseus, who surpassed all the sons of Erechtheus, an unseen bond beneath the earth of Taenarus kept him back, for he had followed Peirithous on that fateful journey — otherwise the two of them would have made the toil of the quest easier for all.

Tiphys, son of Hagnias, left behind the people of Siphae...

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK I

not destined to return to Cerinthus. For fate had ordained that he and Mopsus, skilled in the seer's art, should wander and perish in the furthest ends of Libya. For no ill is too remote for mortals to incur, seeing that they buried them in Libya, as far from the Colchians as is the distance between the setting and the rising of the sun.

To him Clytius and Iphitus joined themselves, the guardians of Oechalia, sons of Eurytus the ruthless — Eurytus, to whom the Far-shooting god gave his bow; but he took no joy in the gift, for of his own choosing he strove even against the one who gave it.

After them came the sons of Aeacus, not both together, nor from the same place; for they had settled far from Aegina in exile, after in their folly they had slain their brother Phocus. Telamon dwelt on the Attic island, but Peleus departed and made his home in Phthia.

After them from Cecropia came warlike Butes, son of brave Teleon, and Phalerus of the ashen spear. Alcon his father sent him forth; yet Alcon had no other sons to care for his old age and livelihood. But him, his dearly beloved and only son, he sent forth so that amid bold heroes he might shine with distinction. But Theseus, who surpassed all the sons of Erechtheus, an unseen bond kept beneath the land of Taenarus, for he had followed that path with Peirithous; surely both of them together would have eased the fulfilment of all their toil.

Tiphys, son of Hagnias, left the Siphaean people of

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

...of the Thespians, skilled at reading the swelling wave of the broad sea, skilled at judging the storm-blast of the wind, and at plotting a course by the sun and stars. Tritonian Athena herself urged him into the company of the heroes, and he came among those who longed for him. For she herself had labored to build the swift ship; and Argus, son of Arestor, had constructed it according to her instructions. Because of this it surpassed all other ships that had ever made trial of the sea with oars.

After these came Phlias, from Araithyrea, where he lived in wealth through the favor of Dionysus, his father, dwelling by the springs of the Asopus.

From Argos came Talaus and Areius, sons of Bias, and mighty Leodocus, whom Pero, daughter of Neleus, bore; for whose sake Melampus, son of Aeolus, suffered great anguish in the stalls of Iphiclus.

Nor did we learn that the son of Aeson wished to pass over the mighty Heracles of the bold spirit. But when he heard the report of the heroes gathering, he was coming from Arcadia along the road to Lyrceian Argos, on which he was carrying a live boar that had fed amid the glades of Lampeia, a great wonder of the Erymanthian marsh. He set it down, still bound, from his great shoulders, in the first assembly-place of the Mycenaeans; and he himself, on his own initiative, beyond the intention of Eurystheus, set out. With him went Hylas, his noble squire, in the first bloom of youth, to carry his arrows and to guard his bow.

After him came the offspring of divine Danaus — Nauplius. For he was the son of Clytoneus, son of Naubolus; Naubolus in turn was son of Lernus; and Lernus we know to have been...

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK I

the Thespians, well skilled to foretell the rising wave on the broad sea, and well skilled to infer from sun and star the stormy winds and the time for sailing. Tritonian Athena herself urged him to join the band of chiefs, and he came among them as a welcome comrade. She herself also fashioned the swift ship, and with her Argus, son of Arestor, built it according to her guidance. For this reason it proved the finest of all ships that have ever been tested upon the sea with oars.

After them came Phlias from Araethyrea, where he lived in prosperity through the favor of his father Dionysus, at his home by the springs of Asopus.

From Argos came Talaus and Areius, sons of Bias, and mighty Leodocus — all of whom Pero, daughter of Neleus, bore; and on her account the Aeolid Melampus suffered great hardship in the cattle-yard of Iphiclus.

Nor do we find that Heracles of the mighty heart ignored the eager summons of Aeson's son. But when he heard news of the heroes' gathering and had reached Lyrceian Argos from Arcadia by the road along which he had carried the boar alive — the boar that fed in the thickets of Lampeia, near the vast Erymanthian swamp — he set that boar down, still bound in chains, from his great shoulders at the entrance to the marketplace of Mycenae; and then of his own free will set out against the wishes of Eurystheus. With him went Hylas, a brave young companion in the bloom of youth, to carry his arrows and guard his bow.

Next to him came a descendant of the race of divine Danaus, Nauplius. He was the son of Clytonaeus, son of Naubolus; Naubolus was son of Lernus;

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

Of Proetus' line, descended from Nauplius: for the Danaid Amymone, having lain with Poseidon, bore Nauplius long before, who surpassed all men in seamanship.
Idmon came last of all who dwelt in Argos, though he knew his own fate from the omens as he went, lest the people begrudge him glory. He was not truly of Abas' blood, but Leto's son himself begat him, numbered among the glorious sons of Aeolus; and he himself taught him to read the prophecies of birds and to observe the signs of burnt offerings.
And Leda, the Aetolian woman, sent mighty Polydeuces and Castor, skilled in the management of swift-footed horses, from Sparta; she bore these cherished sons in a single labor in the halls of Tyndareus, and she did not refuse when they came to go, for she had in mind the honor worthy of Zeus's bed.
And the sons of Aphareus, Lynceus and overbearing Idas, came from Arene, both brimming with great courage; Lynceus surpassed all with the sharpest of eyes — if the tale is true — and could easily see a man even beneath the surface of the earth.
And with them Periclymenus the Neleid set out to join the voyage, the eldest of all the sons born to divine Neleus at Pylos; Poseidon had granted him boundless strength and whatever he might pray for in the thick of battle, to transform himself.
And Amphidamas and Cepheus came from Arcadia, who inhabited Tegea and the estate of Apheidas, two sons of Aleus; and a third followed them as they went — Ancaeus, whom his father Lycurgus sent, being the elder brother of both of them. But he already...

This passage from Book I of the Argonautica describes the gathering of the Argonauts. Lernus was the son of Proetus, son of Nauplius; and Amymone, daughter of Danaus, once married to Poseidon, bore Nauplius, who surpassed all men in seamanship. Idmon came last among those who lived at Argos. Although he had learned through augury that he would die on the voyage, he came anyway, so that people would not begrudge him his fame. He was not truly the son of Abas, but Apollo himself had fathered him to be counted among the noble Aeolids, and had taught him the art of prophecy — reading the flight of birds and interpreting the signs in burnt offerings. From Sparta, the Aetolian Leda sent the mighty Polydeuces and Castor, skilled in guiding swift horses — her beloved twin sons, born together in the house of Tyndareus. She did not hold them back from going, for her thoughts were worthy of one who had been the bride of Zeus. Lynceus and proud Idas, sons of Aphareus, came from Arene, both glorying in their great strength; and Lynceus in particular excelled in sharpness of sight — if the story is true that this hero could see clearly even through the earth itself. With them came Periclymenus of Pylos, eldest of all the godlike sons of Neleus born at Pylos. Poseidon had given him boundless strength and the ability to take on whatever form he desired in the heat of battle. From Arcadia came Amphidamas and Cepheus, who lived in Tegea on the land once belonging to Apheidas — both sons of Aleus — and Ancaeus followed them as a third, sent by his father Lycurgus.

He left aging Aleos and the city, to bring back his son and entrust him to his own brothers. He set out wearing the bear-skin of Maenalus, and in his right hand he wielded a great double-edged axe. For his grandfather Aleos had hidden his armor in a deep recess of the storehouse, hoping somehow to prevent him still from making the voyage.

Augeas also came, he whom rumor called a son of Helios; he ruled as king over the men of Elis, and gloried in his wealth; he greatly longed to see the land of Colchis and Aeetes himself, the lord of the Colchians.

Asterius and Amphion, sons of Hyperasius, came from Achaean Pellene, which their grandfather Pelles once founded on the heights above Aegialus.

Next, leaving Taenarus, Euphemus arrived, swiftest of all men in foot-speed, he whom Europa, daughter of mighty Tityos, bore to Poseidon. That man could run over the swell of the grey sea, and never wet his swift feet, but skimming along on just the tips of his toes, he sped across the watery path.

Two other sons of Poseidon also came: one was Erginus, who had left the city of noble Miletus, and the other was Ancaeus the mighty, from Imbrasus, the seat of Hera, in Parthenia; both claimed skill in seamanship and boasted of prowess in war.

After these, Meleager, the valiant son of Oeneus, came up from Calydon, and Laocoon with him — Laocoon, brother of Oeneus, though not by the same mother, for a slave woman had borne him. Oeneus sent him now, already old, as guardian of his son. Thus still in his youth Meleager entered the bold company.

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK I

brother older than both. But he was left in the city to look after Aleus, who was growing old, while he sent his son to join his brothers. Ancaeus went dressed in the skin of a Maenalian bear, wielding a huge double-edged battleaxe in his right hand. His grandfather had hidden his armor in the innermost recess of the house, hoping by some means to prevent his departure.
There also came Augeias, whom rumor declared to be the son of Helios; he ruled over the Eleans and gloried in his wealth, and he greatly wished to see the land of Colchis and Aeetes himself, the ruler of the Colchians.
Asterius and Amphion, sons of Hyperasius, came from Achaean Pellene, which Pelles, their grandfather, had once founded on the heights of Aegialus.
After them came Euphemus from Taenarus, the swiftest of men on foot, born to Poseidon by Europe, daughter of mighty Tityos. He could skim across the swell of the grey sea and never wet his swift feet, but just touching the surface with his toes was carried along the watery path.
And two other sons of Poseidon came as well: Erginus, who left the citadel of glorious Miletus, and proud Ancaeus, who left Parthenie, the seat of Imbrasion Hera; both claimed great skill in seamanship and in war.
After them came from Calydon the son of Oeneus, the great Meleagrus, and Laocoon — Laocoon, the brother of Oeneus, though not by the same mother, for a serving-woman had borne him. Now growing old, Oeneus sent him to watch over his son; and so Meleagrus, still a young man, joined the bold band of heroes. No other

15

of heroes. I think no other man surpassed him, except Heracles, had he come — if only he had not spent that year among the Aetolians and been transformed by his stay there. And indeed his maternal uncle, well skilled to face an opponent with the javelin and equally skilled in close combat, Iphiclus the son of Thestius, accompanied him on the same journey.

With them came Palaemonius, son of Lernus of Olenus — called son of Lernus by repute, though his birth was truly from Hephaestus; and because of this his foot was lame, but no one could find fault with his body or his valor, and so he was counted among all the best heroes, adding glory to Jason.

From the Phocians came Iphitus, born of Naubolus, son of Ornytus; he had been Jason's guest-friend before, when Jason came to Pytho to ask the oracle about the voyage, for Iphitus had received him in his own home.

Then came Zetes and Calais, the sons of Boreas, whom Oreithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, once bore to Boreas on the far edge of wintry Thrace — where Thracian Boreas had snatched her up from Cecrops' land as she danced beside the Ilissus. He carried her far away, to the place known as the Sarpedonian rock, beside the stream of the river Erginus, and there he mastered her, wrapping her in dark clouds. These two, as they rose up, beat their dusky wings on either side of their feet — a wondrous sight to behold — gleaming with golden scales; and about their backs, from the crown of the head and along the neck on either side, their dark locks streamed in the blasts of wind.

Nor indeed was Acastus, son of mighty Pelias himself, content to remain in his father's halls —

had come superior to him, I think, except for Heracles, if for one more year he had stayed and been raised among the Aetolians. Yes, and his uncle, well skilled in fighting whether with the javelin or hand to hand, Iphiclus son of Thestius, accompanied him on his way.
With him came Palaemonius, son of Olenian Lernus — Lernus by reputation, but his birth was actually from Hephaestus; and so he was crippled in his feet, but no one would dare scorn his physical frame and his courage. For this reason he was counted among all the chiefs, winning glory for Jason.
From the Phocians came Iphitus, descended from Naubolus son of Ornytus; he had once been Jason's host when Jason went to Pytho to seek an oracle about his voyage, and there Iphitus welcomed him in his own halls.
Next came Zetes and Calais, sons of Boreas, whom Oreithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, once bore to Boreas on the edge of wintry Thrace — the very place to which Thracian Boreas had snatched her away from Cecropia while she was whirling in the dance, close by the stream of Ilissus. Carrying her far off to the place men call the rock of Sarpedon, near the river Erginus, he wrapped her in dark clouds and took her by force. There the two brothers were growing their dusky wings, which quivered upon their ankles on both sides as they grew — a great wonder to behold, wings that gleamed with golden scales; and around their backs from the top of the head and neck, here and there, their dark locks were being tossed by the wind.
Nor did Acastus, son of mighty Pelias himself, have any wish to remain behind in his father's palace,

to stay behind — Argus, the helper of the goddess Athena. These two were also destined to be enrolled in the company.

Such were the comrades who gathered to the son of Aeson. All the neighboring peoples called them the Minyae, one and all, since most and best of them boasted descent from the blood of the daughters of Minyas; and so too Jason's own mother Alcimede, born of Clymene the daughter of Minyas, had given him birth.

Now when the servants had made all ready aboard — everything that well-equipped ships are fitted with within, when need drives men to sail across the sea — then the heroes made their way to the ship through the city, to where the shore of Pagasae of Magnesia is enclosed. Around them the people thronged and surged together. The heroes shone out like bright stars gleaming among clouds; and each man who watched them rushing past in their armor spoke thus:

"Zeus our king, what is Pelias thinking? Where is he driving so great a company of heroes out beyond the land of all the Greeks? They could burn Aeetes' palace with consuming fire on the very day they arrived, if he does not willingly give them the Fleece. But the road cannot be fled from, and the toil for those who go is without end."

So people spoke here and there throughout the city. And the women raised their hands again and again to the immortals in the air, praying that they might grant a joyful homecoming. One wept to another, lamenting:

"Poor Alcimede, evil has come to you too at last, though late, and you have not fulfilled your life in happiness."

nor Argus, helper of the goddess Athena; but they too were ready to be counted among the company.

So many, then, were the helpers who gathered to join the son of Aeson. All the chiefs whom the people of that region called Minyae — for the most part and the bravest of them claimed descent from the blood of the daughters of Minyas; and thus Jason himself was the son of Alcimede, who was born of Clymene, the daughter of Minyas.

Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls — all the things that fully-equipped ships require when men's business takes them across the sea — the heroes made their way through the city to the ship where it lay on the strand that men call Magnesian Pagasae. A crowd of people came hurrying together, but the heroes shone like gleaming stars among the clouds, and each man who saw them speeding along in their armor would say:

"King Zeus, what is Pelias's purpose? Where is he driving forth from the Panachaean land so great a host of heroes? In a single day they could lay waste the palace of Aeetes with destructive fire, should he refuse to yield them the fleece of his own free will. But the road is not one to be avoided — the toil is hard for those who dare it."

So people spoke here and there throughout the city; but the women often raised their hands to the sky in prayer to the immortals to grant a safe return, the desire of their hearts. And one among them lamented with tears to her companion:

"Wretched Alcimede, evil has come upon you at last, though late — you have not ended your days in glory."

Aeson too was deeply wretched. Indeed it would have been better for him if, laid out in burial rites beforehand, he had lain beneath the earth, still ignorant of his troubles. Would that the dark wave had swept away Phrixus too, along with the ram, when the maiden Helle perished; but the evil omen gave forth a human voice, so that it might lay up grief and countless sorrows for Alcimede hereafter.'

Such were the words the women spoke as they went to the entrance gates. Already many male and female servants had gathered, and his mother clung about him, overcome with grief. Sharp anguish pierced each one of them; and with them his father, wrapped in helpless old age, lay groaning upon his bed, covered up. But Jason then soothed their distress, encouraging them, and told the servants to lift the warrior's arms; and they, downcast, lifted them in silence. His mother, as she had at first thrown her arms around her son, clung to him weeping more intensely, like a girl who joyfully falls upon her aged nurse when she is alone, a nurse who has no other guardians left, but drags out a hard life under a stepmother who has recently oppressed her with many insults — and the girl's heart within is bound fast by grief as she weeps, nor can she pour out as much lamentation as she longs for. So Alcimede wept bitterly, holding her son in her arms, and spoke these words in her anguish:

'Would that on the day when I, wretched woman, heard King Pelias proclaim his wicked command, I had at once breathed out my life and forgotten all my cares, so that you yourself might have laid me out with your own dear hands,

"My child — for that was the one wish I still had left
from you, while all the other gifts of nurture I have long since spent —
now I, once admired among Achaean women,
shall be left in my halls like an empty-handed slave,
wasting away in longing for you, ill-fated me, through whom I had
great glory and renown before, and for whom alone
I first and last loosened my bridal girdle. For to me above all
did Eileithyia, the goddess of birth, begrudge many children.
Woe to my folly — I never imagined, not even in a dream,
that Phrixus would bring ruin upon me by his escape."

So she wailed and lamented; and her attendant women
wept around her one by one. But Jason spoke to her
with gentle, comforting words:

"Do not heap upon me such bitter griefs,
mother, like this — for you will not hold back misfortune
with tears; you would only add sorrow upon sorrow.
For the gods dispense hidden sufferings to mortals;
bear your share of them with patience, even though your heart aches.
Take courage from the pledges of Athena,
and from the oracles, since Phoebus gave very favorable signs,
and besides that, from the aid of the heroes.
But you, stay here quietly in your home
among your handmaids — do not be like an ill-omened bird for the ship;
companions and servants will accompany me on my way."

So he spoke, and set off from the house to go forward.
As Apollo goes forth from his fragrant temple,
over sacred Delos, or to Claros, or to Pytho,
or to broad Lycia by the streams of Xanthos —
just so did he move through the crowd of people; a cry rose up
from all sides together. And the aged woman met him

thine own hands, and might have buried me; for that was the only wish I had left to be fulfilled by you. All the other rewards for raising me I have long enjoyed. But now I, once so admired among Achaean women, shall be left behind like a slave in my empty halls, wasting away in grief, ill-fated as I am — and all for love of you, the one for whose sake I once had such splendour and renown, you, my only son, for whom I gave up my virginity first and last. For the goddess Eileithyia grudged me abundant offspring more than she did any other woman. Alas for my foolishness! Not once, not even in my dreams, did I foresee that the flight of Phrixus would bring me such misery."
With these words she wept and moaned, and her handmaidens standing by lamented with her; but Jason spoke to her gently with words of comfort:
"Do not, I beg you, mother, store up too much bitter sorrow, for you will not rescue me from danger with your tears — you will only add grief to grief. The sorrows that the gods deal out to mortals are unseen; be strong enough to endure your share of them, even with grief in your heart. Take courage from the promises of Athena and from the responses of the gods — for Phoebus has given very favorable oracles — and then from the support of the chieftains. But stay here quietly among your handmaids, and do not be a bird of ill omen for the ship; my clansmen and servants will follow me there."
With that he set out and left the house. And as Apollo goes forth from some fragrant shrine — whether to sacred Delos, or Claros, or Pytho, or to broad Lycia near the stream of Xanthus — in just such beauty did Jason move through the crowd of people, and a great cry rose as they all shouted together. And there to meet him came aged

for all her desire, as the crowd pressed forward;

But when he had left the well-built streets of the city
and reached the Pagasaean shore, his companions
received him there, waiting together beside the ship Argo.
He stood at the gangway, and they gathered to face him. 320
When they noticed Acastus and Argus coming down
from the city apart from the others, they were astonished to see them
rushing in full haste, contrary to Pelias's intention.
Argus, son of Arestor, had wrapped around his shoulders
a bull's hide reaching to his feet, dark with its shaggy hair; the other wore
a fine double cloak that his sister Pelopeia had given him.
Even so, Jason held back from questioning them both about everything,
and bade them all gather in assembly.
There, leaning against the sail and the mast,
they all sat down in a row one after another. 330
And the son of Aeson spoke to them with goodwill:
"All the other things that need to be fitted out on the ship—
everything is in good order—lies ready
for our departure.
So we would not delay on that account
our voyage, whenever the winds alone breathe fair.
But, friends—for the return to Greece is shared among us,
and shared are our paths to the land of Aeetes—
therefore now, setting aside all hesitation, choose the best man

leader of our company, to whom the management of each matter would belong, and to settle quarrels and agreements with strangers."

So he spoke; and the young men looked to bold Heracles where he sat among them, and with one voice they all called on him to lead. But he, from where he sat, stretched out his right hand and spoke:

"Let no one offer me this honor. I will not agree to it, and I will also hold back any other who rises to claim it. Let the man who assembled this company be its leader."

So he spoke, full of pride, and they agreed, as Heracles urged. And warlike Jason himself rose up gladly, and spoke thus to those who were eager:

"If indeed you entrust this honor to my care, then let our course no longer be delayed as before. Let us now first propitiate Phoebus with sacrifices and set about preparing a feast nearby. And while my estate managers, whose task it is to drive choice cattle here from the herds, are on their way, let us haul the ship into the sea, stow all the tackle aboard, and assign the oarsmen to their benches by lot. Meanwhile, let us also build a shoreside altar to Apollo of Embarkation, who promised me under entreaty that he would guide and show me the sea-routes, if I begin my contest with sacrifices in his honor."

So he spoke, and was the first to turn to the work. The others rose and followed his lead. They piled their garments in heaps on a smooth flat rock which the sea's waves did not reach, though in winter the salt spray had long since washed it clean.

Following Argus' instructions they first girded the ship within by stretching a well-twisted rope on either side, so that the timbers might be held firmly together by the bolts and withstand the force of the sea-surge. They quickly dug out a channel as wide as the space the ship occupied, and as far in from the prow as the sea would reach when she was dragged down. They kept digging it lower and lower in front of the keel, and in the trench they laid polished rollers; then they tilted the ship forward onto the first of the rollers, so that she would glide along over them. High up on either side they turned the oars around and lashed them, projecting a cubit's length beyond the thole-pins. The men themselves took their stations on both sides, pressing with chests and hands together. Then Tiphys stepped aboard to urge the men to heave at the right moment; calling out loudly, he gave the signal. At once, throwing their full weight into it, they thrust her forward with a single mighty effort, straining their feet against the ground as they drove forward. And the Pelian Argo sped swiftly along; the men on either side shouted as they rushed forward. The rollers groaned beneath the heavy keel as it ground over them, and dark smoke curled up from the friction; she slid down into the sea, and the men held her back with their hauling-ropes to keep her moving forward at a controlled pace.

They fitted the oars into the thole-pins on both sides, and stowed aboard the mast and well-made sails and all the ship's provisions.

After they had carefully attended to each of these things, they first assigned the rowing benches by lot, two men to each; but the middle bench they set apart without casting lots for Heracles and, among the heroes, for Ancaeus, who dwelt in the city of Tegea. These two alone they left the middle bench, and with acclamation entrusted Tiphys to hold the steering oar of the well-keeled ship.

Then, heaping up shore-pebbles nearby, they built there an altar on the beach to Apollo, surnamed Actius and Embasius; and quickly they spread dry olive logs upon it. Meanwhile the herdsmen of Aeson's son drove up and brought two oxen from the herd. The younger companions drew these near the altar, and then brought water for the ritual hand-washing and the barley for scattering. And Jason prayed, calling upon his ancestral Apollo:

"Hear me, Lord, you who dwell in Pagasae and in the city named for Aeson my father, you who at Pytho promised me, when I came in need, that you would reveal the completion and the end of the journey — for you yourself were the cause of these trials — now guide the ship yourself, with my companions safe, there and back again to Hellas. And in return, as many of us as shall return, we will lay glorious sacrifices of bulls again upon your altar; and other abundant gifts I will bring to Pytho, and others to Ortygia. Now go, and accept this offering from us, Far-Shooter."

This we offered first to you as the tribute for boarding your ship; may I loose, O lord, the cables by your favor on a propitious fate, and may a gentle breeze blow, by which we shall sail over the sea in fair weather.'

He spoke, and with his prayer cast the barley-meal. And the two girt themselves over the oxen — mighty Ancaeus and Heracles. The one struck the bull mid-brow about the forehead with his club, and it fell in a heap and sank to the ground; the other, cutting the other ox across the broad neck with his bronze axe, severed the mighty sinews, and it crashed down, its horns striking the earth on both sides. The comrades quickly slaughtered them, flayed the hides, cut up the flesh and carved it, and cut out the sacred thigh-pieces; these they covered together thickly with fat and burned upon split logs. And the son of Aeson poured unmixed libations over them, and Idmon rejoiced as he watched the flame blazing on every side from the offerings, and the smoke rising in purple spirals — a favorable omen. Straightway he declared without reserve the mind of Apollo's son:

'For you it is fated by the gods' will and destiny to cross to the place and bring back the fleece; and there are countless trials both on the way there and on the return. But for me, it is decreed that I die somewhere far off on the Asian mainland by a hateful doom of fate. Even so, knowing this ill from the omens I had read before, I left my homeland to embark on the ship, so that glory might remain upon my house for my having sailed.'

So he spoke; and the young men, hearing the prophecy, rejoiced at the news of their return, but grief took hold of them at Idmon's fate.

When the sun passes the steady midpoint of day, and the fields are freshly shadowed by the cliffs as it tilts toward evening darkness, then at last they all spread a deep bed of leaves on the sand along the shore of the grey sea and lay down in rows. Beside them lay countless provisions and sweet wine, drawn off by the wine-pourers with ladles. Afterward they took turns in speaking to one another, as young men often do at a feast with wine, taking their pleasure when reckless insolence is absent.

But there Jason, son of Aeson, was troubled within himself, brooding over everything, looking like a man cast down. Idas, perceiving this, rebuked him with a loud voice:

"Son of Aeson, what plan are you turning over in your mind? Speak your thought aloud among us all. Or does creeping fear grip you — that thing which unnerves cowardly men?

Let my fierce spear bear witness, by which I win glory beyond all others in battle, and Zeus helps me no more than my own spear does — let no disaster befall us, no quest go unfulfilled while Idas follows along, even if a god should oppose us. Such is the champion you bring from Arene."

So saying, he took up a brimming cup in both hands and drank the sweet unmixed wine; his lips and dark beard were wet with it. All of them murmured together, and Idmon spoke out openly:

"Reckless man, you devise ruin for yourself as well as for others. Does the undiluted wine swell your bold heart in your chest with madness, and has it driven you to treat the gods with contempt?"

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

There are other words of comfort, such as a man might use to encourage a comrade; but you have spoken utter recklessness. Such talk as this once stirred the sons of Aloeus to boast against the blessed gods — men to whom you are not even remotely equal in valor — and yet they both were slain by the swift arrows of the son of Leto, mighty though they were."

So he spoke; and Idas, son of Aphareus, laughed aloud in scorn, and squinting at him replied with mocking words:

"Come then, tell me this by your prophetic arts — whether the gods will bring upon me too such a doom as your father dealt to the sons of Aloeus. Consider how you might escape my hands alive, if I catch you delivering empty prophecies."

He raged and taunted him; and the quarrel would have gone further, had not their comrades and Aeson's son himself called them sternly to order; and Orpheus raised his lyre in his left hand and made trial of song.

He sang of how earth and sky and sea, once joined together in a single form, were separated apart from one another by deadly strife; and of how the stars, the moon, and the paths of the sun hold their fixed course forever in the sky; and of how the mountains rose, and how the roaring rivers with their nymphs came into being, and all creeping things. He sang of how first Ophion and Eurynome, daughter of Ocean, held power over snowy Olympus; and how through force and strength he yielded his honor to Cronus and she to Rhea, and they fell into the waves of Ocean; while those two ruled over the blessed Titan gods in the meantime,

36

While Zeus was still a boy, still knowing only childish thoughts, he dwelt beneath the Dictaean cave; and the earth-born Cyclopes had not yet armed him with the thunderbolt, with thunder and lightning — for these are what give glory to Zeus.

Then he [Orpheus] held back his lyre together with his divine voice. But they still stretched their heads forward even after he had stopped, all alike motionless on upright ears, held in enchantment — such was the spell his song had left upon them. Not long after, having poured libations to Zeus, as is right and proper, over flaming tongues, they turned their thoughts through the darkness toward sleep.

But when radiant Dawn with her bright eyes looked upon the steep peaks of Pelion, and the headlands, washed by the sea, grew calm as the waves subsided, then Tiphys woke, and at once roused his companions to board the ship and make ready the oars. The harbor of Pagasae and the Argo of Pelion herself gave a terrible cry, urging them to set sail — for driven into her keel was a divine beam that Athena had fitted from a Dodonian oak. The men took their places on the benches in order, as they had apportioned their rowing stations before, and sat in good order beside their gear. In the middle sat Ancaeus and mighty Heracles; beside him he placed his club, and beneath his feet the ship's keel sank low in the water. The mooring ropes were already being hauled in, and they poured wine over the sea. But Jason, weeping, turned his eyes away from his native land.

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

Just as young men in honor of Phoebus set up a choir at Pytho, or perhaps at Ortygia, or by the waters of Ismenus, and in unison strike the ground rhythmically with swift feet around his altar to the sound of the lyre — so they smote the rough water of the sea with their oars to the music of Orpheus' lyre, and the waves washed over them. On either side the dark brine seethed with foam, roaring terribly with the might of those powerful men. The heroes' armor flashed like fire in the sunlight as the ship sped on, and her long wake gleamed white behind her, like a path seen crossing a green plain.

On that day all the gods looked down from heaven upon the ship and upon the strength of the demigod heroes, who were then the finest men sailing the sea. Upon the topmost peaks the Nymphs of Pelion stood in wonder, gazing at the work of Athena of Iton and at the heroes themselves swinging the oars in their hands.

And Chiron, son of Phillyra, came down from the high mountain to the edge of the sea, and dipping his feet in the surf, waved his great hand again and again in farewell, wishing them a safe and trouble-free return. His wife was with him, carrying on her arm the infant Achilles, son of Peleus, to show him to his dear father.

When they had left behind the curving shore of the harbor, guided by the skill and wisdom of Tiphys the son of Hagnias — who expertly handled the well-planed steering oar to keep the ship on a steady course — they then stepped the great mast in its socket and made it fast with forestays, stretching them taut on either side,

They poured the lines down from it, drawing them onto the spindle. A sharp breeze fell upon them, and having fastened the halyards around the smooth cleats, one on each side, they sailed calmly past the long headland of Tisaia.

For them, playing his lyre in tuneful song, the son of Oeagrus sang of Artemis, fair-fathered guardian of ships, who watched over those lookout points of the sea and protected the land of Iolcus. And fishes from the deep, leaping up above the sea, great and small mixed together, followed along, bounding through the watery paths. As when countless flocks follow in the tracks of a rustic shepherd, sated full with grass, heading to the fold, while he goes ahead playing a lovely pastoral tune on his clear-sounding pipe — so the fish accompanied them, and an ever-freshening breeze carried the ship onward.

At once the misty, grain-rich land of the Pelasgians sank from sight; they sped ever onward past the steep cliffs of Pelion; the headland of Sepias disappeared, Sciathus appeared rising from the sea, and in the distance appeared Peiresiai and the sun-drenched coastal shore of Magnesia and the tomb of Dolops. There, toward evening, driven back by counter-winds, they put in to shore, and honoring him with offerings of sheep by night, they lay encamped while the sea's swell rolled. For two days they rested on the beach, but on the third they launched the ship, having spread aloft the great sail. That shore is still called the Launching-place of Argo.

From there they ran onward past Meliboea,

...passing along the stormy headland and the shore,
and at dawn they sighted Homole close at hand,
sloping to the sea, and coasted past it; nor did they wait long
before clearing the mouth of the river Amyros.
Then they gazed upon the Eurymenae and the wave-washed ravines
of Ossa and Olympus; and after that
the slopes of Pallene, rounding Cape Canastraeum,
they pressed on through the night, running before the wind.      600
At dawn, as they sailed on, the Thracian headland of Athos
rose before them — Athos, whose topmost peak
casts its shadow over Lemnos, though that island lies
as far away as a well-rigged merchantman could sail by midday,
as far even as Myrina.
For them the whole day and on into the dark a strong,
utterly favoring wind blew and the ship's sail was spread full.
But with the first rays of the sun, when the wind had fallen,
they came by rowing to rocky Lemnos, isle of the Sintians.

There the entire population had been mercilessly laid low         610
in the year just past by the transgressions of the women.
For the men, having grown to hate their lawful wives, had rejected them
and were possessed by a fierce passion for the captive girls
whom they themselves had brought back from raids across the water
into Thrace; for the dread wrath of Aphrodite pursued them,
because for a long time they had dishonored her with their offerings.
Wretched women! Consumed insatiably by jealousy —
they slew not only their husbands along with those slave-women
in their beds, but every male creature together, so that
in time to come no one could exact vengeance for the grim slaughter.
Only Hypsipyle alone, of all of them, spared her aged father        620
Thoas, who had been king throughout the land;

In a hollow chest he set him to drift upon the sea, in case he should survive. The sailors first hauled him to Oenoe, but later the island was called by another name — Sicinos — after Sicinus, whom the Naiad nymph Oenoe bore to Thoas when she lay with him.

To those women, tending herds of cattle and donning bronze armor, and cleaving the grain-bearing fields, was easier than all the works of Athena at which they had formerly busied themselves. Yet even so they often gazed with terrified eyes out over the broad sea, in dread whenever the Thracians might come.

So when they saw the Argo being rowed near the island, they immediately streamed out beyond the gates of Myrina in full force, clad in war-gear, onto the shore — like raw-flesh-eating Thyiads — for they supposed it was the Thracians who were arriving. And along with them Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, put on her father's armor. They stood speechless, so great was the fear that hung over them.

Meanwhile the heroes sent swiftly from the ship their herald Aethalides, to whom were entrusted messages and the staff of Hermes, his father on both their sides, who had granted him imperishable memory of all things. Not even now, though he has gone down to the unspeakable eddies of Acheron, has forgetfulness crept over his soul; but his memory endures always, alternating — at one time counted among those beneath the earth, at another returning to the light of the sun among living men. But why must I tell at length the story of Aethalides? He it was who at that time persuaded Hypsipyle to welcome the arrivals.

...through the darkness of the dying day; nor at dawn did they loose the ship's cables to the breath of the north wind.

The Lemnian women went through the city and gathered in the assembly, for Hypsipyle herself had summoned them. And when they had all come together in a crowd, she at once rose among them and urged them, saying:

"Dear friends, come, let us send the men pleasing gifts, such as it is fitting to bring aboard ship — provisions, and sweet wine — so that they may stay steadily outside the walls and not follow us out of need and come to know us truly, and a bad reputation spread far and wide. For we have done a great deed, and it will not be at all pleasing to them either, if they should learn of it. This, then, is the plan I have put forward; but if any of you can devise a better word, let her rise — for it is for this very reason I have called you here."

So she spoke, and sat down on her father's stone seat. Then her dear nurse Polyxo stood up, hobbling on shriveled aged feet, leaning on a staff, eager to speak. Near her sat four unmarried girls, their white hair just beginning to grow. She stood in the middle of the assembly, and barely raised her neck from her bent back, and spoke thus:

"The gifts, as Hypsipyle herself approves, let us send to the strangers, since it is better to give them. But what plan have you for sustaining life, if the Thracian army should press hard upon us, or some other enemy — as many troubles come upon mankind? Just as even now this company has arrived unexpectedly."

But if one of the blessed gods should avert that fate, and countless sufferings worse than war still await in the future — when the older women have wasted away and the younger ones, childless, reach hateful old age — how then will you survive, poor wretches? Will oxen yoke themselves of their own accord to your deep fields and draw the earth-cutting plow through the fallow, and at the turn of the year reap the harvest? As for me, though even now the Fates still make me shudder, I believe that within this year I shall be laid in the earth, having received my due portion of burial rites, as is right, before misfortune comes upon me. But to the younger women I urge that all this be carefully considered. For now at your feet stands a ready means of escape, if you will entrust your homes and all your possessions to the strangers and let them have care of your splendid city.'

So she spoke, and the assembly was filled with noise. For her words pleased them. Then after her Hypsipyle rose up again and spoke in reply:

'If this desire pleases all of you, I would now send a messenger to the ship.'

So she spoke, and called to Iphinoe who was standing near: 'Go for me, Iphinoe, to meet the man who leads this expedition, and bid him come to our home, so that I may declare to him a message pleasing to the people; and call upon the men themselves to come with goodwill onto our land and into our city, if they so wish.'

With that she dissolved the assembly and set off to return to her own house. And likewise Iphinoe came to the Minyans. They asked her,

You might more easily cast your eyes toward the rising sun than gaze upon that crimson splendor. For the middle of it was wrought in deep red, while the edges were entirely purple; and at each border many intricate figures were skillfully embroidered throughout.

On it were the Cyclopes, seated at their immortal work, forging the thunderbolt for lord Zeus; it was by now almost complete and gleaming, but still lacked a single ray, which they were hammering out with iron mallets, breathing out the raging breath of fire.

Next to this was wrought deep-tressed Cytherea holding the swift shield of Ares; and from her shoulder the fastening of her tunic had slipped loose down along her left arm beneath her breast; and opposite, the true likeness of it appeared to be seen reflected in the bronze shield.

He set out toward the city, like a bright star that rises above the rooftops, watched by young brides shut within their new-built chambers, and which casts its spell upon their eyes through the dark blue air as it glows beautifully, while a maiden longs for the youth who is away among foreign men — the youth her parents are keeping for her as a bridegroom. Like that star, the hero made his way along the path before the city. When they had entered within the gates and the town, the common women crowded behind him, rejoicing in the stranger. But he, fixing his eyes on the ground, walked straight ahead until he reached the splendid palace of Hypsipyle. Her attendants flung open the double doors when he appeared — doors fitted with well-crafted planks. There Iphinoe led him swiftly through the fair colonnade and seated him in a gleaming chair opposite her mistress. She cast her eyes aside and blushed upon her girlish cheeks; yet despite her shyness she addressed him with these winning words:

"Stranger, why did you linger so long outside our walls, sitting there idle? For the city is not inhabited by men — rather, settlers from the Thracian mainland plow the wheat-bearing fields. I will tell you the whole truth about our misfortune, so that you yourselves may know it well."

When my father Thoas reigned as king over the people here, the men of Thrace, who dwell over against us, would raid the farmsteads of the community from their ships, and bring back here endless plunder along with captive girls. The scheming of the destructive goddess Cypris was at work, casting upon the men a madness that destroyed their hearts. For they had come to hate their wedded wives, and driven by their folly had driven them from their homes, while they lay with their war-won slave-women — the wretches. Long we endured it, hoping they might at some point come to their senses again; but the evil doubled and kept growing. Their lawful children were dishonored in the halls, and a shadowy brood was rising up. Unwed girls and widowed mothers wandered through the city uncared-for. A father would not spare a thought for his own daughter, even if he watched her being torn apart before his very eyes by the hands of a cruel stepmother. Nor did sons any longer defend their mother, as before, against shameful outrage. No brother gave a thought to his sister in his heart. Instead, those slave-girls were all that mattered — in the house, in the dances, in the assembly, and at the feasts — until some god cast into our hearts an audacity beyond all bounds: that when the Thracians returned from their campaign we would no longer receive them within our walls, so that they might either come to their senses as was right, or else depart and go elsewhere to settle with their slave-women. And so they took with them whatever male children remained in the city, and went back, and even now they inhabit the snowy farmlands of Thrace.

But come now, go to your ship and tell your companions our words, and do not linger outside the city.'

So she spoke, concealing the end of the slaughter that had befallen the men. Then he answered her in turn:

He spoke, and touched her right hand, and quickly turned to go back. And around him countless maidens thronged from every side rejoicing, until he passed out through the gates. Afterward the women rode down to the shore in smooth-rolling wagons, bearing many gifts of hospitality, when Hypsipyle had summoned him and reported the whole story without break; and they readily led the men themselves to their homes as guests. For Cypris stirred up sweet desire, as a favor to crafty Hephaestus, so that Lemnos might be peopled again with men in time to come, unspoiled.

There then the son of Aeson made his way to the royal house of Hypsipyle; the others went wherever each one happened to lodge, apart from Heracles, for he had been left behind by the ship.

praying to the blessed gods to grant a safe return. And so too Hypsipyle prayed, clasping the hands of the son of Aeson, while tears streamed down her cheeks at his departure:

Then the son of Aeson answered her with words of comfort: "Hypsipyle, may all these blessings come to pass from the blessed gods. So he spoke, and was the first to step aboard the ship; and likewise the other heroes embarked, and took the oars in their hands, sitting in order. Argos loosed the stern-cables from the salt-spray-beaten rock. And then they —

they struck the water mightily with their long oars. Toward evening, at the bidding of Orpheus, they put in at the island of Electra, daughter of Atlas, so that by learning her gentle, sacred rites they might sail more safely over the chilling sea. Of these matters I will say no more; but may the island itself rejoice, and those divine spirits who hold those mysteries as their lot — rites which it is not lawful for us to sing.

From there, rowing through the depths of the Black Sea, they kept the land of Thrace on one side and Imbros above them on the other; and just as the sun was setting they reached the jutting headland of the Chersonese. There a swift south wind blew for them, and setting their sails to the breeze they entered the swift currents of the daughter of Athamas; the open sea was left behind them by morning, and in the night they measured out the waters within the shore of Rhoiteion, keeping Idaean land on their right. Leaving Dardania they made for Abydos, and past it they skirted Percote and the sandy beach of Abarnis and sacred Pityeia. In that same night, as the ship drove on, they crossed the Hellespont swirling with eddies.

There is a steep island deep within the Propontis, a little off from the rich-soiled mainland of Phrygia, sloping toward the sea, where an isthmus low and flat is washed by the waves and spreads along the shore. It has twin shores, and lies above the waters of the Aesepus; the people dwelling round about call it the Mountain of the Bears.

And there dwell violent and savage Earth-born creatures, a great wonder for the neighboring peoples to behold; for each has six mighty arms, two growing from their sturdy shoulders, and four below, fitted most terribly along their sides. The Doliones, moreover, inhabited the isthmus and the plain — men among whom the hero Cyzicus, son of Aeneus, ruled, whom Aenete, daughter of divine Eusorus, had borne. The Earth-born, fearsome as they were, did the Doliones no harm, by the aid of Poseidon, for the Doliones were originally sprung from his line. There the Argo drove forward, urged on by Thracian winds, and the Fair Harbor received her as she sped along. There, on the advice of Tiphys, they left the small anchor-stone beneath a spring — the spring of Artacia — and took another, a heavy one, that served well. That former stone the Neleian Ionians later consecrated as a holy relic, as was right, in the sanctuary of Jasonian Athena. The Doliones and Cyzicus himself, meeting them all together, when they heard who the expedition was and what their lineage, welcomed them with hospitality, and persuaded them as they rowed onward to moor their stern-cables in the harbor of the city. There the heroes set up an altar to Apollo of the Embarkation upon the shore, and attended to the sacrifice. The king himself gave them sweet wine and sheep together; for there had come to him a prophecy that whenever a divine band of hero-warriors arrived, he should at once meet them with kindness and have no thought of war.

Yet even so, leaving the chamber and the bed of his bride, he busied himself with the feast among them, and cast fear from his heart.

And they questioned one another in turn. He on his part inquired about the voyage and the commands of Pelias; while they asked him about all the cities and gulf of the wide Propontis; but he could not tell them fully all they desired to know. At dawn they climbed the great Dindymon, so that they themselves might look upon the passages of that sea; and from there they had driven the ship from her former anchorage to the Chytus harbor; and that path is called the Jasonian road, even that which they trod.

But the Earth-born giants from the other side rushed down from the mountain and blocked the sea-mouth of the Chytus harbor with rocks from below, as though lying in wait for a beast within. But Heracles had been left there with the younger men, and he quickly drew his back-bent bow and brought them down one after another to the earth; and they too themselves hurled jagged rocks. For indeed the goddess Hera, wife of Zeus, had reared those terrible monsters as a labor for Heracles. And the others too, turning back before they had reached the lookout point, joined in the slaughter.

When the heroes had accomplished their fearless contest, they loosed the ship's cables and sped forward through the swell of the sea before the wind's breath. She ran all day under sail; but as night came on, the steady wind held no longer, and counter-blasts swept them violently back until they came again to the hospitable Doliones. They went ashore that very night; the rock is still called Sacred, to which they had hastened to make fast the ship's cables. So he who thought himself beyond the reach of ruinous destruction was bound by it that very night as he fought; and many other defenders fell: Heracles slew Telecles and Megabrontes; Acastus cut down Sphodris; Peleus took Zelys and the swift warrior Gephyrus. They rushed in a throng to the gates; and swiftly the city was filled with the uproar of the terrible battle's return. At dawn both sides recognized the deadly and irreparable mistake; and a dreadful grief seized the Minyan heroes when they saw Cyzicus, son of Aeneus, lying before them in the dust and blood. For three whole days they mourned and tore their hair, both the heroes themselves and the Doliones together. Then three times they marched in arms around his tomb and performed the funeral rites, and they competed in the games, as is customary, on the grassy plain where even now
