Nor was Cleite, wife of the fallen king, left behind after her husband's death; on top of her grief she carried out something still more terrible, fastening a noose about her neck. And the woodland nymphs themselves lamented her death; all the tears they shed from their eyes upon the ground the goddesses fashioned into a spring, which they call Cleite — the glorious name of that unhappy bride. Most dreadful of all was that day sent by Zeus upon the Dolion women and men alike; for none of them could bring themselves to touch food, and for a long time in their grief they gave no thought to the work of grinding grain — but kept alive eating their food uncooked. Even now, when the Ionians who dwell in Cyzicus pour their annual libations, they always grind the offering-cake on the communal millstone for all the people.

From that place rough storms arose and kept them there for twelve days and nights together, preventing them from sailing. But on the following night, the other chieftains, overcome at last by sleep, were resting in their final watches, while Acastus and Mopsus son of Ampycus kept watch over those who slumbered deeply. Then over the golden head of Jason's son a halcyon hovered, crying in its clear voice, foretelling the end of the raging winds. Mopsus heard and understood the favorable voice of the shore bird. The god then turned it aside, and it soared up and settled high upon the ornamental stern-post of the ship. Mopsus then went and roused Jason where he lay on soft sheepskin bedding, and spoke to him thus:

"Son of Aison, necessity requires you, as you enter this sacred place on rugged Dindymon, to propitiate the fair-throned Mother of all the blessed gods. Then the fierce storms will cease. For I just now heard this news from the halcyon of the sea, which flew around above you as you slept, revealing everything point by point. For from her come the winds and the sea and all the earth below and the snow-covered seat of Olympus; and when she ascends from the mountains to the great heaven, even Zeus himself, the son of Kronos, gives way to her. And likewise the other immortal and blessed gods revere this dread goddess."

So she spoke, and as he listened, her words were welcome to him. He sprang joyfully from his bed and roused all his companions, urging them on, and told them of the prophecy of Mopsus, son of Ampyx, as they woke. Straightway the younger men drove cattle from the pastures nearby up to the steep summit of the mountain. The others loosed the cables from the sacred rock and rowed to the Thracian harbor, and they themselves came ashore, leaving only a few of the crew aboard the ship. Before them appeared the Makrian heights and all the coast of Thrace visible from where they stood; and there appeared the misty mouth of the Bosporus and the hills of Mysia, and on the other side the flowing river Aisepos, and the city and the Nepian plain of Adrasteia. There was a sturdy vine-stump, thick with growth in the forest, long-rooted and ancient. They cut it down so that it might become a sacred image of the mountain goddess; and Argos shaped it skillfully, and they set it up upon the rugged hilltop, sheltered overhead by the topmost oak trees, which are rooted highest of all.

They passed by an altar of heaped stones, and crowning themselves with oak leaves they attended to the sacrifice, calling upon the Dindymian Mother, much-revered, dwelling in Phrygia, and upon Titias and Cyllenus together, who alone among the many are called the fate-dispensers and attendants of the Idaean Mother, all those who are the Idaean Dactyls of Crete, whom once the nymph Anchiale, grasping the soil of the Dictaean cave with both her hands, brought forth.

And with many prayers Jason besought her to turn away the storms, pouring libations upon the burning offerings. At the same time the young men, at Orpheus's bidding, leaped and danced an armed dance, beating their shields with their swords, so that the ill-omened cry, which the people were still sending up in grief for their king, might be lost in the air. From that time forth the Phrygians propitiate Rhea with the rhombus and the drum.

And the goddess, it seems, put a favorable spirit into their holy sacrifices, and signs fitting to the occasion appeared. The trees poured forth fruit in abundance, and around their feet the earth of its own accord put forth flowers of tender grass. Wild beasts left their lairs and thickets and came fawning with their tails. And she wrought yet another marvel: for never before had water flowed on Dindymus, but then and there a stream gushed forth unceasing from the dry peak. And the neighboring peoples afterward called that spring the Jasonian spring.

And then they set out a feast on the mountains of the Bears in honor of the goddess, singing the praises of Rhea the much-revered. And at dawn, when the winds had ceased, they left the island and rowed away.

Then strife urged on each of the heroes to be the last to stop rowing. For the windless air had smoothed the eddies all around and lulled the sea to rest. Trusting to the calm, they drove the ship forward by sheer strength; and not even the storm-footed horses of Poseidon could have overtaken her as she sped across the deep. Yet when the swell rose again on freshening breezes that spring up from the rivers toward evening, they were already worn out and beginning to slacken — all except Heracles, who with the full strength of his arms was hauling them along as they labored together, and shaking the fitted timbers of the ship. But when, eager to reach the Mysian shore, they were drawing level — just a little way off from Phrygia — with the outflows of the Rhyndacus and the great tomb of Aegaeon, then Heracles, wrenching at his oar-blade against the drag of the rough swell, snapped it in the middle. He fell sideways, clutching half the broken blade in both hands, while the sea swept the other half away on its surging current. He sat up in silence, looking around him — for his hands were unused to being still.

Now at the hour when a vine-digger or a plowman gladly makes his way home to his own farmstead, longing for his supper, and there on his own doorstep sinks his weary, dust-caked knees and looks at his worn hands, cursing his belly for all the grief it brings him — at that very hour they arrived at the land of Cios, at the shores around Mount Arganthon and the mouth of the river Cios. The Mysians, who inhabit that country, received them kindly as they came in friendship, and gave them provisions, sheep, and wine in abundance to meet their need. Then some of the crew went to gather dry firewood, and others soft bedding.

    But the son of Zeus, having given careful instructions to his companions to enjoy the feast, went off into the forest to find an oar that would be ready to his hand when he needed it.
Wandering, he found then a fir tree, not heavily laden with branches nor yet great in its flourishing growth, but like the slender sapling of a poplar — equal in length and thickness to the eye.
Quickly he laid on the ground his quiver, the arrow-holder, along with his bow, and stripped off the lion's skin.
He shook it from the floor with his bronze-weighted club and gripped the trunk with both hands from below, trusting in his strength; planting his feet wide apart, he pressed his broad shoulder against it, and straining close, he wrenched it up from the ground with its deep roots and all the clods of earth clinging to it.
As when a sudden squall strikes a ship's mast unexpectedly, at the time when the deadly setting of Orion is most wintry, and a swift gust from above tears it out together with its wedges from the forestays — even so did he heave it up. Then, gathering up his bow and arrows and his lion's skin along with the club, he turned back to go.

    Meanwhile Hylas, with his bronze pitcher, had gone apart from the company in search of a sacred spring, so that he might be first to draw water for the evening meal and have all else in good order ready for Heracles on his return.

For he himself had reared him in such ways from infancy, having taken him from his father's home — from noble Theiodamas, whom he had slain pitilessly among the Dryopians, when he resisted over his ploughing ox. Theiodamas was cutting the furrows of the fallow field with his plough, stricken with distress; but Heracles bade him yield up the ploughing ox, though he was unwilling. For he sought to cast upon the Dryopians a pretext for grievous war, since they paid no heed to justice in their ways. But let this be driven far afield from our song.

Swiftly he made his way to the spring which the neighboring people call Pegae. And just then the choruses of nymphs were assembling there; for it was the concern of all those nymphs who haunted that lovely slope to sing always by night in honor of Artemis. Those who had their domain on the mountain peaks or in the glens were ranging as wood-wardens from afar; but one, the water-nymph, was rising fresh from the fair-flowing spring, and she saw him nearby, glowing with beauty and sweet grace. For the full moon, shining down from the sky, cast its light upon him. Cypris struck her heart with confusion, and she could barely gather her wits together in her bewilderment. But as soon as he leaned sideways and pressed the pitcher into the stream, the water roared loud all around as it poured into the ringing bronze — and at once she laid her left arm from above upon his neck, longing to kiss his tender mouth; and with her right hand she pulled his elbow, and plunged him into the middle of the whirl.

There stood the cattle-stalls and the court of Amycus, king of the Bebrycians, an arrogant man whom a Bithynian nymph, Melia, once bore to Poseidon Genethlios after lying with him — he who was the most overbearing of men. He had imposed a cruel custom even upon strangers: that no one might depart before trying their hands against his in boxing; and he had slain many of the neighboring peoples. At that time too he came to the ship and, when he needed to inquire about their voyage and who they were, he insulted them with his insolence, and spoke these words aloud among them all:

"Hear me, seafarers — as is fitting for you to know. It is the rule that no stranger who approaches the Bebrycians may depart before raising his hands against mine in combat. Therefore, choose out from your company your best man, and let him stand here on the spot to contend with me in boxing. If you defy my laws and trample them underfoot, then grim and mighty compulsion will come down hard upon you."

So he spoke, full of arrogance. But those who heard him were seized by fierce anger, and the taunt struck Polydeuces above all. Swiftly he stepped forward as champion of his comrades and called out:

"Hold now — and do not show us your vaunted strength in cruelty, whoever you claim to be. We will submit to your rules, as you proclaim them. I myself willingly pledge here and now to face you."

There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his house by the sea — he who had endured the most terrible of all sufferings on account of the gift of prophecy which the son of Leto had granted him long before. He had not even the slightest reverence for Zeus himself when he revealed the sacred will of the god truthfully to men. Therefore Zeus visited upon him an endless old age, and took from his eyes their sweet light, and would not allow him to take joy in the boundless provisions that his neighbors always gathered and brought to his home as they sought oracles. But suddenly swooping through the clouds close at hand, the Harpies would continually snatch the food from his mouth and hands with their hooked beaks. Sometimes not even a scrap of food was left him, sometimes only a little, so that he might live on in misery. They would also pour a foul stench over what remained, and no one could bear even to approach — one had to stand far off, so rank was the stench that breathed from the remnants of his meal.

"First of all, setting out from me, you will see the two Cyanean Rocks in the straits of the sea; of these I say that none has ever passed through unscathed. For they are not fixed on their lowest foundations, but frequently rush together face to face, and above them much seawater surges up boiling; and the roar crashes fiercely around the rugged shore.

Now be persuaded by my counsel, if truly you are sailing with sound minds and with regard for the blessed gods; and do not destroy yourselves with a self-chosen doom through recklessness, rushing on driven by the impetuosity of youth. First, try the test by sending a dove ahead from the ship toward the rocks. If she flies through safe on her wings to the open sea, then no longer hold back yourselves from the passage, but grip your oars firmly in your hands and cleave the narrow sea-strait; for the light will be of far less help than the strength of your arms. So let all else go and labor above all at this with boldness. I do not forbid you to pray to the gods before that. But if the dove perishes midway flying straight through, turn back; for it is far better to yield to the immortals. You could not escape a grim fate from the rocks, not even if the Argo were made of iron.

O wretched men, do not dare to go beyond my divine warnings, even if you think me thrice as hostile to the sons of Uranus as I am, and even more hated — do not dare to sail past the omen of the bird. What will happen will be as it must be. But if you escape through the Clashing Rocks unharmed into the Pontic sea, keeping the land of the Bithynians on your right hand immediately,

The goddess graciously granted them the oaths, and they dove in fear into the vast cave of the Dictaean cliff. Then all the companions were overjoyed in the halls, as was Phineus himself at the news. And the son of Aeson addressed him with great warmth:

"Surely then, Phineus, some god did care about your dreadful suffering, and has brought us here from far away, so that the sons of Boreas might defend you. And if he could also restore light to your eyes, I think I would rejoice as much as if I were returning home."

So he spoke, and Phineus answered him with downcast eyes:
"Son of Aeson, that cannot be undone, nor is there any remedy for it hereafter; for my empty eye sockets smolder away. But instead of that, may a god grant me swift death, and dying I shall share in all glories."

So the two of them spoke in turn with one another. And before long, as they were still exchanging words, Dawn appeared. Around Phineus the neighboring men gathered, who had always come there daily, continually bringing him a share of their own food. To all of them the old man gave his prophecies generously, whoever came, even the most humble, and he freed many from their troubles through his oracular skill; and for this reason they would come to tend to him. Among them came Paraebius, who was the dearest to him; and Phineus was glad to see these men in his halls. For already some time before, he himself had foretold to them, as the company of the best men of Hellas was setting out toward the city of Aeetes, that they would moor their cables in the Thynian land, and that from Zeus would come those who would hold back the Harpies as they came.

Then the old man dismissed them with reassuring words, but bade Paraibios alone to remain there with the chief men; and he urged him to bring back whichever of his own sheep was the finest. As that man went forth from the hall, Phineus spoke gently to the assembled oarsmen:

"Friends, not all men are arrogant after all, nor unmindful of good deeds. Such a man as this came here to learn his own fate. For just when he had toiled and suffered more than most, need of life's necessities wore him down ever more relentlessly; day after day his hardship grew worse, and there was no respite for him in his distress. Yet he was paying the grim penalty for his father's sin. For his father, cutting timber alone in the mountains, once disregarded the pleadings of a Hamadryad nymph, who with tearful, urgent words begged him not to cut the trunk of an oak tree that had lived so long, for she had spent her long life within it without ceasing. But in the reckless arrogance of youth he cut it down. So the nymph brought a fate that brought no gain upon him and his children afterward. When he arrived before me, I recognized the sin; I bade him build an altar and offer propitiatory sacrifices upon it to the Thynian nymph, praying to escape his ancestral doom. And when he escaped the god-sent destruction, never did he forget me or disregard me; though he is eager to remain with me in my distress, I can barely bring myself to send him away unwillingly."

So spoke the son of Agenor. The man quickly came driving two sheep from the flock. And Jason rose up,

And the sons of Boreas went up at the old man's bidding. Quickly, calling upon Apollo for an oracle, they made sacrifice upon the hearth-stone at the dawn of the new day. The younger companions prepared a satisfying feast. Then, having feasted well, some lay down to sleep by the ship's cables, and others gathered together in the halls right there.

At dawn the Etesian winds blew down upon them — those winds which, by the command of Zeus, blow across all the earth alike in this same way.

There is a story that Cyrene tended her flocks beside a marsh of the Peneius, in the company of men of former times; for maidenhood and an unsullied bed were dear to her. Apollo, catching her up as she was herding far from Haemonia, entrusted her to the earthly nymphs who dwelt near the Myrtosian cliff in Libya. There she bore to Phoebus Aristaeus, whom the prosperous Haemonians call Agreus and Nomius. The god made her an immortal nymph of that place, a huntress; and he brought their infant son to be raised in the cave of Chiron. When Aristaeus had grown to manhood, the divine Muses betrothed him and taught him the arts of healing and of prophecy; they also made him keeper of their flocks, all those that grazed across the Athamantian plain of Phthia and around the steep slopes of Othrys and the sacred stream of the Apidanus.

But when Sirius blazed down from heaven upon the Minoan islands, and the inhabitants found no remedy for their long affliction, then at the bidding of the Far-Shooter they called upon him to ward off the plague. He left Phthia at his father's command and settled in Ceos, gathering the people together.

...of Parrhasia, who are of the lineage of Lycaon, and he built a great altar to Zeus Ikmaios, and duly offered sacrifices in the mountains to that star Sirius and to Cronos' son Zeus himself. By his will the Etesian winds from Zeus cool the earth for forty days; and still now in Ceos the priests offer sacrifices before the rising of the Dog Star.

So much for those traditions. The heroes remained there, kept back by delay; and the Thynians day after day brought countless gifts to Phineus out of good will. Then, building an altar to the blessed gods on the far shore of the breaking sea and setting offerings upon it, they embarked on the swift ship to row onward, and they did not forget to take with them the trembling dove. Euphemus held her, terrified, in his hand, and they loosed the double mooring lines from the land.

Nor did Athena fail to notice them as they set out. Swiftly she stepped onto a light cloud that could carry her quickly despite her weight, and sped toward the sea, with kindly thoughts for the oarsmen. As when a man wandering far from his homeland — as we mortals often wander in our endurance — and no land is too distant, all roads lie visible in his mind's eye, and he imagines his own home, and at once the wet sea-path and the dry land appear before him, and now one, now another flashes sharply before his searching eyes: so the daughter of Zeus darted swiftly and set her feet on the Thynian shore of the Inhospitable Sea.

When they reached the narrow mouth of the winding passage, hemmed in on both sides by jagged rocks, while the churning current surged beneath their advancing ship...

The current swept the ship, and gripped by fear they rowed forward with great speed. Already the crash of the clashing rocks fell ceaselessly on their ears, and the sea-washed shores resounded. Then at that moment Euphemus rose and stepped to the prow, gripping the dove in his hand, while the crew, at the command of Tiphys son of Hagnias, bent willingly to their oars so that they might drive through the rocks, trusting in his strength. As the rocks opened they caught sight of the outermost curve of the passage. Their hearts melted within them. But Euphemus sent the dove darting forward on her wings, and they all together raised their heads to watch. She flew through between the rocks, and the rocks, clashing back against each other, crashed shut on both sides at once. A great spray of brine was churned up like a cloud, and the sea roared terribly, and the vast air thundered all around.

The hollow caverns boomed beneath the rough sea-crags as the sea surge washed within them, and high on the cliff the white foam of the breaking wave sprang upward. Then the current swept around the ship in a swirl. The rocks clipped the tail-feathers of the dove at the tips; but she flew on unharmed. The oarsmen shouted aloud, and Tiphys himself cried out to row with all their might, for the rocks were opening again. But as they pulled, trembling seized them, until the returning backwash of the flood carried the ship in between the rocks itself. Then the most terrible dread seized them all, for destruction beyond all help hung over their heads. Already on either side the broad Pontus opened to view, and suddenly before them a great arching wave reared up without warning, steep as a sheer cliff. When they saw it

they bowed their heads sideways. For it seemed about to leap over the whole ship and overwhelm it. But Tiphys anticipated it, easing off as the oar-blades grew heavy, so that the great wave rolled away beneath the keel; and he drew the ship itself back from the rocks at a distance, and it was carried aloft, suspended in mid-air. Euphemus went along among all the crew calling them to throw their whole strength upon the oars; and they struck the water with a shout. But as much as the ship gave way beneath the rowers, twice as much did it spring back; and the oar-blades bent like curved bows under the force of the heroes' pulling.

Then immediately after that a towering wave rushed forward, and she ran like a cylinder before the raging sea, plunging headlong through the hollow brine. In the midst of the Clashing Rocks the swirling current held her; and the rocks on either side thundered as they swayed, and the ship's timbers were held fast. Then Athena with her left hand thrust back the solid rock, and with her right drove the ship through to pass on her way. She shot forward lofty as a winged arrow. Yet even so the onrushing rocks sheared off the tips of the stern-ornament as they crashed together. But Athena sprang up to Olympus when they had escaped unscathed. The rocks then were rooted fast together in one place, close against each other, permanently — for so it had been fated by the blessed gods, whenever anyone should see them and pass through by ship. The heroes for a moment breathed again from their chilling terror, gazing out at the sky and the wide expanse of sea spread out afar. For they felt they had escaped from Hades. Tiphys was the first to speak:

"I expect that this very ship will safely carry us through; nor is any other so responsible as Athena, who breathed divine strength into it when Argus was fitting it together with bolts — it is not fated to be destroyed. And, son of Aison, since the god has granted us escape through the Rocks, fear no such thing further; for Phineus, son of Agenor, said that the trials ahead would be easy to accomplish."

With these words she drove the ship onward through the open sea past the Bithynian shore. But Jason addressed Tiphys beside him with gentle, reproachful words:

"Tiphys, why do you offer me these consolations in my grief? I have made a terrible and ruinous blunder. When Pelias gave his command, I should have refused this expedition outright, even if I was destined to be torn apart and die miserably on the spot. As it is, I am gripped by excessive fear and unbearable anxieties — dreading to sail the icy paths of the sea, and dreading whenever we set foot on land. Everywhere there are hostile men. Night after night I lie awake in misery, ever since you first gathered here on my behalf, turning each thing over in my mind. You speak easily enough, caring only for your own life; but as for me, I have no fear at all on my own account — it is for him and likewise for you and all the other companions that I tremble, if I cannot bring you safely back to the land of Greece."

So he spoke, testing his men. They responded with words of encouragement. His heart was warmed within him by their cheering, and he spoke to them again openly:

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

"Friends, it is in your courage that I find strength.
Therefore, not even if I were setting out through the very depths of Hades would I now be seized by fear, since you remain steadfast amid terrible dangers. But since we have sailed past the Clashing Rocks, I believe there will no longer be another such fear ahead — if indeed we make our way back guided by the counsel of Phineus."

So he spoke, and straightway they ceased from such words and bent unceasingly to the toil of rowing. Swiftly they passed the swift-flowing river Rhebas and the crag of Colone, and not long after, the headland of Melaina, and then the mouths of the Phylleian stream, where Dipsacus, son of Athamas, had in former times welcomed the heroes into his own home, when Phrixus fled with the ram from the city of Orchomenus. A meadow-nymph had borne him; violence was not to his liking, but willingly by his father's waters he dwelt with his mother, tending flocks along the shore. His sacred precinct they quickly passed, and also the broad banks of the river, the plain, and deep-flowing Calpe — and through day and into calm night they drove on with tireless oars.

As when toiling oxen cleave the sodden field, and measureless sweat streams down from their flanks and necks, and their eyes roll sideways under the yoke, and a dry gasping blows endlessly from their mouths, and all day long they labor driving their hooves into the ground — so did the heroes haul their oars out of the sea.

At that hour when the immortal light has not yet come, nor is the darkness still deep, but a thin gleam has run over the night — that time which those who rise early call the half-light of dawn —

At that time, sailing into the harbor of the desolate island of Thynia, they stepped ashore worn out with heavy suffering.
To them appeared the son of Leto, passing far above on his way from Lycia to the boundless land of the Hyperborean people; golden clusters of hair streamed on either side of his cheeks as he moved along; in his left hand he carried a silver bow, and a quiver hung stretched across his shoulders down his back; beneath his feet the whole island shook, and waves washed up over the dry land. An overwhelming amazement seized those who saw him; no one dared to look directly into the god's beautiful eyes. They stood with heads bowed toward the ground, while he passed on far away through the air over the sea. At last Orpheus spoke these words to the heroes, declaring:

"Come now, let us consecrate this island as sacred to Apollo of the Dawn, since he appeared to all of us as he passed by at daybreak. We will perform such rites as are within our means, raising a coastal altar. And if he grants us a safe homeward journey to the land of Haemonia, then at that time we will lay on his altar the thigh-pieces of horned goats. But for now I urge that we appease him with burnt offerings and libations. Be gracious, lord, be gracious, you who have appeared to us."

So he spoke, and straightway some of them built an altar of stones, while others ranged over the island searching to see if they might spot any deer or wild goats, such as often graze in the deep woodland. The son of Leto provided them with game, and from all of it they reverently burned double portions of thigh-pieces on the sacred altar, singing the praises of Apollo of the Dawn. Around the burning offerings they set up a wide choral dance,

singing "Hail, Iepaion! Iepaion, Phoebus!"
and with them the noble son of Oeagrus
led the song on his Bistonian lyre with its clear tone —
how once beneath the rocky ridge of Parnassus
he slew with his arrows the mighty Delphyne,
still a youth, still unclad, still rejoicing in his long locks.
"Be gracious! Ever, O lord, your hair remains uncut,
forever inviolate — for so it is right. Only Leto,
daughter of Coeus, fondles it with loving hands."     710
And the Corycian nymphs, daughters of Pleistus,
called out "Ieie!" and gave him many words of encouragement;
and so from that time this fair refrain belonged to Phoebus.

When they had honored him with choral song,
they swore solemn oaths over pure libations
that they would always stand by one another
in harmony of heart, touching the sacrifices;
and even now that shrine of gracious Concord stands there,
which they themselves built at that time, honoring that most glorious deity.

When the third dawn appeared, they then     720
left the steep island on a fresh west wind.
From there, passing by the opposite mouth of the river Sangarius
and the rich land of the Mariandynians,
and the streams of the Lycus and Lake Anthemoeis,
they sailed on, watching; and beneath the wind's breath
all the ropes and tackle of the ship shook as they went.
At dawn, when the wind had lulled through the dark of night,
they gladly reached the harbor of the Acherusian headland.
It rises sheer with towering cliffs,
looking out over the Bithynian sea; and beneath it     730
smooth sea-washed rocks are rooted in the deep;
around them the rolling surf thunders loud;
and above, at the very top, wide-spreading plane trees have grown.

150

From it, set back inland, lies a hollow open glen, where there is a cave of Hades, roofed over with forest and rock, from which a freezing breath, exhaled from the chilly depths without ceasing, has always formed a white frost all around — one that melts only at noon under the midday sun. Never does silence hold that grim headland, but there is a constant murmur from the sea and from the rustling of leaves in the hollow recesses. Here too are the outpourings of the river Acheron, which bursts through the headland and discharges into the eastern sea; a hollow gorge brings it down from above. In later times the Nisaean Megarians named it Soonautes ("Savior of Ships"), because it had saved them — ships and all — when they were battered by a terrible storm. So then the heroes beached their ship right there, beyond the Acherusian headland, as the wind had just died down.

Nor did they go long unnoticed by Lycus, the lord of that land, or by the Mariandynian men, once they set out — men who had killed Amycus, as the fame of it had already reached them. So the people made a pact of friendship with them on that account. They welcomed Polydeuces himself as though he were a god, gathering from all sides, since for a long time they had been at war against the arrogant Bebrycians. And so that very day, going into the city, they feasted in Lycus's halls in friendship and gladness, cheering their hearts with conversation. Jason told him the lineage and name of each man,

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

He told them of their own companions' deeds, of Pelias' commands, of how they had entertained the Lemnian women as guests, of all they accomplished around Cyzicus among the Doliones, of how they came to Mysia and to Cios, where they left the hero Heracles against their will, and he related the prophecy of Glaucus, and how they destroyed the Bebrycians and Amycus, and told of Phineus' oracles and his sufferings, and how they escaped the Clashing Rocks, and how they encountered the son of Leto on the island. And as he told each thing in order, the king was charmed at heart as he listened; but grief seized Heracles' companions at his being left behind, and he spoke these words to them all:

'Friends, what a man's help you have been parted from as you attempt this long voyage to Aeetes! For I know him well, having seen him in person in the halls of Dascylus my father, when he came here on foot through the continent of Asia, carrying the war-belt of Hippolyte; and he found me then just beginning to show the first down on my cheeks. There, on the occasion of our brother Priolas having been killed by Mysian men — a man for whom the people still lament with most pitiful dirges even now — he defeated in contest the powerful boxer Titias, who was outstanding among all the young men in looks and in strength, and knocked his teeth to the ground. And together with my father he subdued the Mysians, and also the Phrygians, who farm fields neighboring ours, and he won dominion over the tribes of Bithynia along with the very land itself, as far as the streams of Rhebas and the crag of Colone; and the Paphlagonians of Pelops' line likewise submitted,

...as many as the dark water of the Billaeus encircles. But now the Bebryces and the arrogance of Amycus, dwelling far off, have robbed me of Heracles' territory, cutting off a great deal of land, until they pushed their boundary as far as the deep-flowing meadows of Hypius. Even so, they have paid the penalty at your hands; and I do not think that on this day, against the will of the gods, Ares was brought upon the Bebryces, when the son of Tyndareus slew that man. So then they spent the whole day feasting together. At dawn they went down to the ship in haste, and Lycus himself went with them, having given countless gifts to carry, and at the same time he sent his son to go with them from the house.

Then fate drove Idmon, the son of Abas, skilled in prophecy, to his doom — yet his prophetic arts did not save him, since necessity led him to be destroyed. For a white-tusked boar, a deadly monster, lay cooling its flanks and vast belly in the mud in the reedy marsh of the river, and even the very
[text continues on next page]

The marsh-dwelling nymphs were seized with fear, and no man knew how the boar grazed across the wide swamp. But the son of Abas made his way up along the muddy banks of the river; and the boar, leaping up unseen from the reeds at a great height, struck his thigh, slicing through the sinews to the bone. Crying out sharply, he fell to the ground, and his companions rushed together at his cry with a shout. Peleus swiftly hurled his javelin at the deadly boar as it fled toward the marsh, and charged after it; but Idas struck him, and with a roar the boar fell upon his swift spear. They left that one lying where he had fallen on the ground, and carried the other, who was at his last breath, back to the ship, grieving, and laid him in the hands of his own companions.

Then they held back from the business of sailing, and remained there in distress, occupied with the funeral rites of the dead. They mourned for three full days, and on the next they gave him a great burial; and the people together with King Lycus joined in the funeral honors, and slaughtered the countless sheep that custom demands for the departed. A tomb was heaped up there in that land for that hero, and a marker stands for later generations to see — a beam of wild olive wood; it flourishes in leaf a little below the heights of the Acherusian shore. And if I must also speak out plainly what the need of the Muses requires: Phoebus revealed to the Boeotians and Nisaeans that they must earnestly propitiate this guardian of the city, and around that beam of the ancient wild olive tree

to destroy a city; and in place of the god-fearing son of Aeolus, Idmon, they still to this day honor Agamestor.

Who else then died? For once again the heroes heaped a burial mound over a fallen comrade. For two markers of those men are still visible. The story goes that Tiphys, son of Hagnias, died; nor was it his fate to sail any farther on. But him too a wasting sickness lulled to sleep far from his homeland, while the crew was performing the burial rites over the corpse of the son of Abas. They took on a grief unbearable upon that dreadful calamity. For when they had duly buried this man as well, right there on the spot, falling helpless before the sea, they lay wrapped in quiet misery, with no thought of food or drink; their spirits drooped with grief, since the hope of a homeward voyage had grown very distant.

And they would have lingered even longer in their despair, had not Hera breathed extraordinary courage into Ancaeus, whom Astypalaea bore to Poseidon beside the waters of Imbrasus; for he surpassed all others in skill at the helm. He came quickly to Peleus and addressed him:

"Son of Aeacus, how can it be honorable for us, who have not shrunk from toil, to linger long in a foreign land? It is not so much as a man skilled in war that Jason leads me so far from the Parthenius in quest of the fleece, but rather as one who knows ships well. Let there be no fear at all in my mind concerning the ship. And there are other skilled men here too; whichever of them we set at the stern will not fail the voyage. Come then, quickly, urge them with these words and boldly rouse them to remember their mission."

So he spoke; and the heart of Peleus leaped with joy. Without much delay he spoke out among them all.

"You fools, why do we hold to this pointless grief? Those men have met the fate that fell to them. But we still have helmsmen among our company, and many of them. So let us not delay our venture — rise to action, casting aside your sorrows."

But the son of Aeson, at a loss, spoke to him in reply:
"Son of Aeacus, where then are these helmsmen? The very men we used to boast were skilled have now fallen into greater despair than I. And so I foresee a terrible ruin for us together with the dead, if we are to have no hope of reaching the city of murderous Aeetes, or of returning again to the land of Hellas beyond the rocks — and shameful doom will cover us here, growing old to no purpose."

So he spoke. And Ancaeus eagerly undertook to steer the swift ship, for the god had turned his heart to it. After him, Erginus and Nauplius and Euphemus sprang up, each eager to take the helm. But his companions held them back, and the greater number approved Ancaeus.

Then at dawn on the twelfth day they set out, for a great following wind from the west was blowing for them. Swiftly they crossed the Acheron with their oars, and then, trusting to the wind, they spread the sail and cut their way forward at speed, with the canvas stretched wide and fair weather around them. Quickly they came to the mouth of the river Callichorus, where men say the son of Zeus, the Nysaean god, when he had left the tribes of India and settled at Thebes, held his rites and established his dances before the cave in which he spent those holy, joyless nights.

...from which those who dwell around the river Callichorus and the cave of Aulius derive the name. [910]

From there they caught sight of the tomb of Sthenelus, son of Actor, who on his return from the fierce battle against the Amazons—for he had gone to war alongside Heracles—was struck by an arrow and died there on the shore close to the sea. They would not have sailed further on, for Persephone herself sent up the tear-laden soul of Sthenelus, son of Actor, beseeching them to let him look just a little upon men of his own kind. Standing on the mound's rim, he gazed out at the ship just as he had been when going into battle; and around him his fine four-crested helmet gleamed with its crimson plume. [920] Then he sank back into the great darkness, and those who had seen him were struck with awe. Mopsus, son of Ampycus, urged them, as the seer among them, to put in to shore and to appease the shade with libations. They quickly furled the sail, cast out the mooring lines onto the beach, and gathered around the tomb of Sthenelus, pouring libations over it and consecrating the cut offerings of sheep. They also built an altar apart from the libations to Apollo, lord of ships, and burned the thighbones; and Orpheus dedicated his lyre there—and from that the place takes the name Lyre.

Then straightaway, the wind urging them on, they boarded the ship; hauling down the sail they stretched it out to both sheets, and she was carried out to sea under full tension, swift as a hawk that high up through the air spreads its wings and is borne by the breeze swiftly, never beating its pinions, gliding at ease on the still air. And now they reached the salt-washed currents of the Parthenius...

of the gentlest river, which Leto's daughter measures out, she who goes up to heaven when she has refreshed her body in its lovely waters. Then pressing on without pause through the night they sailed past Sesamon and the steep Erythini, Cromyela, Cromna, and wooded Cytorus. From there, rounding Carambis at the rays of the rising sun, they rowed on with their oars along the long shore all day and through the night as well.

Straightway they set foot on the Assyrian land, where Zeus himself had settled Sinope, daughter of Asopus, and had granted her her virginity, beguiled by his own promises. For he had desired her love, and had nodded assent that he would give her whatever she wished in her heart. And she cunningly asked him for her maidenhood. In the same way she deceived Apollo when he sought to lie with her, and the river Halys too; nor did any man ever master her in his longing embrace.

There at that time the sons of noble Deimachus of Tricca — Deileon, Autolycus, and Phlogius — were dwelling, having been separated from Heracles. When they caught sight of the company of heroic men, they came forward and truthfully made themselves known. They no longer wished to remain there any longer, but stepped aboard the ship as the white north wind blew strongly. Together with them, borne on the swift breeze, they left the river Halys behind, left the nearby-flowing Iris too, and the alluvial plain of Assyrian land; and on that same day they rounded, from afar, the headland that shelters the harbor of the Amazons.

They pass by the river where Artemis bathes after hunting, then sail through the night past Sesamus, Erythini, Crobialus, Cromna, and woody Cytorus. They then land on the Assyrian shore at Sinope, whose story is told: Zeus desired her and promised to give her whatever she wished, but she cleverly asked for her virginity, thus outwitting him. She similarly outwitted Apollo and the river-god Halys, and remained forever a virgin. At Sinope they find the sons of Deimachus of Tricca — Deileon, Autolycus, and Phlogius — who had been left behind since the time of Heracles' expedition. Recognizing the heroes, these men come forward and identify themselves, and wishing to leave, they board the ship as soon as the northwest wind blows. The Argonauts then sail past the river Halys and the river Iris and the delta of Assyria, and by the end of the same day they round the far headland of the Amazons that stands at the entrance to their harbor.

But in the topmost tower the king of the Mossynoikoi sits enthroned, dispensing straight judgments to his many people — a wretched arrangement, for if ever he errs in giving a verdict, they shut him in there and keep him starving for the rest of that day.

Sailing past them and drawing near to the opposite shore of the island of Ares, they cut through the sea with their oars all day long; for a gentle breeze died away as evening came on. And now they caught sight of one of the island's resident Ares-birds swooping down through the air above them; it shook its wings over the speeding ship and sent a sharp feather shooting at the crew. The feather fell on the left shoulder of noble Oileus, who dropped his oar from his hands at the blow. His companions stared in wonder at the winged missile. His bench-partner Eribotes pulled the feather out, bound up the wound, and used as a bandage the strap that had hung from his own scabbard. Then a second bird appeared flying after the first, but the hero Clytios son of Eurytus — for he had already drawn his curved bow — shot a swift arrow at the bird and struck it; it spun around and fell close by the swift ship.

Then Amphidamas, son of Aleos, spoke to them: "The island of Ares is near us; you can see that for yourselves from these birds. But I do not think arrows will be enough to get us ashore safely. Let us devise some other helpful plan, if you intend to land there, as Phineus directed. For not even Heracles, when he came to Arcadia, was able to drive away the Stymphalian water-birds from their lake with his bow — I myself witnessed that. Instead, he stood on a high lookout point and made a din by shaking a bronze rattle in his hands, and the birds fled in panic."

...shrieking afar off in panicked fear. With this in mind, let us now devise some such plan; and I myself will tell what came to me before. Put on your heads the high-crested helmets, and half of you row in turns, while the other half cover the ship with spears and shields. Then all together with a great din raise her up on high, so that the birds may be frightened by the unfamiliar sight — the nodding crests and the spears poised above. And if we reach the island itself, then at that point raise a tremendous crash with your shields and a great clamor.'

So he spoke, and his plan pleased everyone. They put bronze helmets on their heads, gleaming terribly, and the scarlet crests tossed upon them. Some rowed in turns; the others covered the ship with spears and shields. As when a man tiles over an enclosure with pottery, to be the glory of his house and a defense against rain, fitting each piece securely next to the last — so they roofed the ship over with their shields locked together. As the clamor that rises from the tumult of fighting men when the battle-lines clash, such was the noise that rose up into the air above the ship. They saw no more of the birds — but when they drew close to the island and clashed their shields, immediately the birds flew up in countless numbers, scattering this way and that through the air. As when the son of Cronus sends down a thick hailstorm from the clouds upon a city and its houses, and the inhabitants sitting beneath their roofs hear the clatter of the hail above them and stay quietly indoors — for the winter season did not catch them unprepared, but beforehand they had strengthened their roof —

like thick-feathered wings they kept hurling at them as they darted on high over the sea toward the mountains of the land.

What then was Phineus's intention, to bring the divine company of heroes to shore here? And what benefit would come to them in their longing afterward?

The sons of Phrixus were sailing back from Aea toward Orchomenus, away from Aeetes of Cytae, having boarded a Colchian ship, to win the boundless wealth of their father — for as he lay dying he had charged them with this journey. And on that very day they were quite close to the island. But Zeus stirred up the strength of the north wind to blow, signaling through the rain the wet season of Arcturus. During the day the wind, blowing gently, shook the leaves on the mountain treetops; but at nightfall it descended upon the sea in full force, roaring with its blasts and raising great waves. A black mist wrapped around the sky, and nowhere could the bright stars be seen through the clouds; a murky darkness pressed in on all sides. The sons of Phrixus, drenched and trembling at their wretched doom, were carried helplessly by the waves. The force of the wind tore away their sails and split the ship itself in two as it was battered by the surge. Then, guided by the will of the gods, the four of them seized a great beam, one of the many that had been scattered when the ship was smashed, fitted together with tight pegs. The waves and blasts of wind carried them, much distressed, toward the island, narrowly escaping death. At once an immense rainstorm broke, drenching the sea and the island and all the land across from it where the overbearing Mossynoeci dwelled. The rush of a wave, together with the great beam,

...cast the sons of Phrixus upon the shores of the island during the murky night. But the endless rain from Zeus ceased with the sunrise, and soon they met one another face to face, and Argos, foremost among them, spoke:

"We entreat you, by Zeus who watches over us, whoever you men may be, to be kind and to give us the help we need. For fierce storms bursting upon the sea shattered all the planks of our wretched ship on which we were sailing our course, having embarked upon an errand. Therefore we now beseech you, if you will hearken, to give us whatever covering for our bodies you can spare, and to take pity on men of your own age in their misfortune. Respect us as suppliants and strangers for the sake of Zeus, god of Strangers and of Suppliants — for both suppliants and strangers belong to Zeus — and he is perhaps watching over us even now."

Then the son of Aeson questioned him wisely, suspecting that the prophecies of Phineus were coming to fulfillment:

"All this we will gladly provide at once. But come, tell me truly: where in the world do you live, and what errand compels you to sail across the sea, and what is your own famous name and lineage?"

Then Argos, helpless in his distress, answered him:

"You have surely heard before now, I think, that one Phrixus, son of Aeolus, came from Greece to Aea — Phrixus, who rode upon a ram to the city of Aeetes, the ram that Hermes had made golden; and you might even now behold the fleece.

But Aeetes is fitted out with terrible and savage cruelties; and because of this I greatly fear the voyage. And it is no easy thing to take the fleece from Aeetes from afar, for such a serpent guards it, all around it, immortal and unsleeping, which Earth herself caused to grow on the slopes of the Caucasus, at the rock of Typhaon, where they say Typhaon, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus the son of Cronos, when he stretched out his mighty hands against him, let fall hot blood from his head; and so he came to the mountains and the Nysian plain, where even now he lies submerged beneath the waters of the Serbonian lake.'

So he spoke; and at once a green pallor spread over the cheeks of many, when they heard of such a labor. But Peleus quickly answered with words of confidence, and said:

'Do not, dear friend, be so utterly dismayed at heart. We are not so lacking in strength as to be found inferior to Aeetes when it comes to the test of arms; and I believe that we too have come there knowing well the ways of war, being sprung from the blood of the blessed gods. Therefore if he will not give the golden fleece in friendship, I do not expect the nations of the Colchians to be of any use to him.'

So they spoke in turn to one another, and then, having satisfied themselves once more with supper, they lay down to sleep. At dawn a fair breeze blew for those who woke; they raised the sails, and these were stretched taut by the rush of the wind; and swiftly they left behind the island of Ares.

Sailing through the night they passed the island of Philyra. There Cronos, son of Ouranos, when he ruled over the Titans on Olympus while Zeus was still being reared in the Cretan cave by the Idaean Curetes, had deceived Rhea and lay with Philyra. The goddess caught them together in that bed; and he, leaping up from the couch, rushed off in the form of a horse with flowing mane. Philyra, the daughter of Oceanos, left that place and those haunts in shame and went to the great mountains of the Pelasgians, where in consequence of that union she bore the monstrous Chiron, half horse, half divine.

From there they sailed past the Macrones, the vast land of the Becheiri, the overbearing Sapeires, and then the Byzeres; pressing ever forward eagerly, borne along by the warm wind. And as they went, the innermost recess of the sea began to open before them. Then the steep crags of the Caucasus rose up, where Prometheus, his limbs bound to the hard rock with bronze chains, fed an eagle on his ever-regenerating liver. They saw it at evening flying with a loud shriek high above the ship, close to the clouds; yet even so it shook all the sail with the blast of its wings as it swept past, for it had not the nature of an ordinary bird of the air, but beat its swift wings like well-polished oars. Not long after they heard the agonized cry of Prometheus as the eagle tore his liver; the air rang with his screams, until once more they saw the ravening eagle flying back the same way from the mountain. In the night, guided by the skill of Argos, they reached the broad-flowing Phasis and the furthest bounds of the sea.

Now the heroes, unseen, were waiting in ambush among the thick reed-beds; but Hera and Athena took notice of them, and, withdrawing apart from Zeus and the other immortals, entered a chamber and took counsel together. Hera was the first to put Athena to the test:
