So she spoke, and Athena answered her at once: "I too, Hera, was turning such thoughts over in my heart when you put the question to me directly. But even now I do not think I have hit upon a plan to strengthen the courage of the heroes, though I have weighed many schemes."
She finished, and the two goddesses fixed their eyes on the ground at their feet, each brooding in silence; and

...divided in their hearts; and straightaway Hera, devising such a plan, spoke first:
'Come, let us go to Cyprus; and approaching Aphrodite together, let us urge her to tell her son, if he will listen, to enchant with his arrows Aeetes' daughter, skilled in many drugs, to fall in love with Jason. For I think that by her guidance he will bring the fleece back to Greece.'

So she spoke; and the shrewd counsel pleased Athena, who replied to her again with gentle words:
'Hera, my father made me ignorant of such shafts, and I know no charm that can compel desire. But if this plan pleases you, then I would follow your lead; but you must be the one to speak when we meet her.'

So saying, they both sprang up and went toward the great palace of Aphrodite, which her lame husband had built for her when he first brought her home as his bride from Zeus. They entered the courtyard and stood beneath the porch of the bedchamber, where the goddess was tending the bed of Hephaestus. But he had gone at dawn to his forge and his anvils, to the wide cavern of the wandering island, where with blasts of fire he worked all his intricate metalwork; and she sat alone in the house upon a carved chair, facing the doors. She had let her hair fall loose over her white shoulders and was combing it with a golden comb, about to braid her long locks. When she saw them before her she stopped, and called them inside, and rose from her chair and seated them on couches; then she herself sat down and, gathering up her uncombed hair with her hands, spoke to them with a smile and in wheedling words:

"Dear ones, what purpose and what need brings you here after so long? You do not usually visit often, since you surpass all goddesses."

Then Hera answered her with these words:
"You mock us. But grief stirs our hearts together. Already the son of Aeson holds his ship on the river Phasis, and with him all those who follow after the Fleece. For all of them, now that the task is near at hand, we are terribly afraid, but most of all for the son of Aeson. Him, even if he should sail down to Hades to free Ixion from his bronze chains below, I will rescue with whatever strength remains in my limbs, so that Pelias may not laugh, having escaped an evil fate — Pelias, who dishonored me by offering sacrifices without my portion. Besides, Jason was dear to me even before this: when at the flooded mouth of the Anaurus, swollen with rain, I tested men's respect for the right, I met him coming back from hunting. All the mountain peaks and high crags were blanketed in snow, and the torrents were rushing down them with a roar. He took pity on me in my guise as an old woman, and lifting me on his own shoulders carried me across the raging water. Therefore he is honored by me without ceasing. And Pelias shall not pay the penalty for his outrage, unless you grant the heroes their homecoming."

So she spoke. Aphrodite was struck speechless by her words. She was awed to see Hera coming to meet her, and then addressed her with gentle words:
"Mighty goddess, may nothing worse befall Aphrodite than your reproach, if I fail to heed your wish in word or deed, whatever these feeble hands of mine can accomplish — and let there be no thought of recompense in return."

So she spoke; and Hera in turn addressed her with shrewd words:
"We have not come in need of force or of hands.
But simply, without a word, entreat your son
to enchant the maiden daughter of Aeetes with desire for the son of Aeson.
For if she in kindness lends him her aid,
I think he will easily win the golden fleece and return to Iolcus,
for she is full of cunning."

So she spoke; and Cypris answered them both:
"Hera and Athena, above all others you might persuade him,
or even I. For shameless as he is toward you,
some small sense of shame will come upon him at your gaze;
but for me he cares nothing, and ever disputes with me and scorns me.
Indeed I have a mind, driven by distraction,
to break his loud-twanging bow and his arrows openly.
For such was his threat when he was angered —
that unless I keep my hands away from him while he still restrains himself,
I should have cause later to blame myself."

So she spoke; the goddesses smiled and looked at each other face to face. And Aphrodite, grieved, spoke again:
"To others my troubles are a cause for laughter; I need not tell everyone — I know it well enough myself.
But now, since this is dear to you both,
I will try, and will coax him, and he will not disobey."

So she spoke; and Hera took her by her slender hand
and said with a gentle smile, glancing sideways at her:
"Just so, Cytherea, do this service now, as you say, quickly;
and do not be vexed or quarrel in anger with your son — he will mend his ways in time."

With that she left her seat; and Athena followed her.
The two departed swiftly back the way they had come. And Aphrodite herself
set off through the folds of Olympus to see if she might find him.

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK III

She spoke, and Hera again addressed her with prudence: "It is not might or strength that brings us here. Simply have your boy enchant Aeetes' daughter into love for Jason. For if she aids him with her clever counsel, I believe he will easily win the golden fleece and return to Iolcus, for she is full of resourcefulness."
Thus she spoke, and Cypris addressed them both: "Hera and Athena, he will obey you sooner than me. Shameless as he is, he will still feel some slight embarrassment before you; but he has no respect for me — he only ever mocks me when he is in a quarrelsome mood. And, worn down by his defiance, I have been on the verge of smashing his loud-twanging arrows and his bow right before his eyes. For in his anger he has threatened that if I do not keep my hands off him while he can still control his temper, I will have only myself to blame afterward."
So she spoke, and the goddesses smiled and looked at one another. But Cypris spoke again, stung to the heart: "To others my troubles are a joke; nor should I be telling them to everyone — I know them all too well myself. But now, since it pleases you both, I will make the attempt and coax him, and he will not refuse me."
Thus she spoke, and Hera took her slender hand and replied with a gentle smile: "Then do this task, Cytherea, right away, as you say; and do not be angry or quarrel with your boy — he will stop tormenting you after this."
She spoke, and rose from her seat, and Athena accompanied her and they went forth together, both hurrying back. And Cypris made her way through the glens of Olympus to find her boy. And she found him apart,

He found him apart in the fertile orchard of Zeus,
not alone, but with Ganymede as well, whom Zeus
had once settled in heaven as a companion to the immortals,
captivated by his beauty. The two of them were playing
with golden knucklebones, as boys of the same age do.
And already reckless Eros was holding the hollow of his left hand
full beneath his breast, standing upright; and sweet
redness bloomed over his cheeks in his complexion.
The other sat crouching nearby in silence, downcast;
he had two knucklebones, and kept tossing one after another
to the other boy, and was angered at his laughter.
He lost these too in quick succession after the ones before,
and went away empty-handed and helpless, not noticing
Aphrodite as she approached. She stood facing the boy
and at once, taking hold of his chin, spoke to him:
  'Why are you smiling, you unspeakable rogue? Did you cheat him
like that, taking unfair advantage of an inexperienced player?
Come now, willingly do me the service I shall name;
and I will give you that beautiful plaything of Zeus,
the one his dear nurse Adrasteia made for him
in the Idaean cave when he was still a babbling infant —
a smooth round ball, better than which you could never get
from the hands of Hephaestus, finer than any.
Its circles are fashioned of gold; around each one
double curved stitching runs in rings;
the seams are hidden; and a dark-blue spiral runs over them all.
But if you toss it in your hands,
it sends a streak of fire blazing through the air like a star.
This I will give you; but you must shoot your arrow at the maiden,
Aeetes' daughter, and enchant her with love for Jason — and let there be
no delay. For the favor would be the weaker for it.'

So he spoke, and the word was welcome to her as she heard it. She cast aside all her soft gifts, and with both hands she clutched the goddess's robe unceasingly, now here, now there. She begged her to go at once in person; and she, meeting her with gentle words, stroking her cheeks, kissed her as she clung to her, and answered with a smile:

"Let my own dear head and yours be witness now that I will indeed give you the gift, and will not deceive you, if you shoot your arrow at the daughter of Aeetes."

She spoke; and he gathered up the knucklebones and counted them all carefully, then dropped them into the bright lap of his mother. Straightway he slung his quiver about him with a golden strap as it leaned against a tree-trunk, and took up his curved bow. He passed through the all-fruited orchard of Zeus's palace, and then went out through the ethereal gates of Olympus. From there a downward path leads through the sky; two mountain peaks, the highest summits of the earth, hold up their heads, where the sun first reddens with his earliest rays as he rises. Below, sometimes the life-giving earth and the cities of men appeared, and the sacred streams of rivers; and sometimes again mountain peaks, while all around the sea spread wide into the air as he traveled.

Meanwhile the heroes were gathered in assembly apart from the ship, sitting in ambush among the reeds along the river. Jason himself addressed them, and they listened quietly, seated there in order in their place:

"Friends, I will tell you what seems best to me myself; as for bringing it to fulfillment, that falls to all of you.

"For the need is shared, and the words are common
to all alike. Let whoever holds back his mind and counsel in silence
know that he alone has robbed this expedition of its homecoming.
Let the rest remain quietly by the ship with their weapons.
But I myself will go to the halls of Aeetes,
taking the two sons of Phrixus and two companions besides.
I will first try him with words in approaching him,
to see whether he would willingly grant us the golden fleece,
or whether he will not, and trusting in his strength, will spurn those who come for it.
For having learned of his hostility from him first,
we will consider whether we shall join battle,
or whether some other plan will aid us if we hold back from that.
Let us not strip him of his treasure by sheer force
before we have even tried words. Better it is
to approach him first and win him over with speech.
For often a word has easily accomplished what
strength could barely achieve, smoothing the way as it was fitting.
Moreover, he once received the noble Phrixus,
fleeing the treachery of his stepmother and his father's sacrifices.
For all men everywhere, even the most shameless,
respect the ordinance of Zeus the God of Strangers and heed it."

So he spoke. The young men approved the words of the son of Aeson
with one accord, and there was no one to propose otherwise.
Then he urged the sons of Phrixus and Telamon and Augeias to follow,
and he himself took the wand of Hermes. At once they went from the ship over the reeds and the water
and stepped out onto the dry land of the rising plain.

This place is called the Kirkaian promontory; and there in a row many black poplars and willows have grown up, on the topmost branches of which corpses hang bound with cords. For even now it is a sin among the Colchians to burn dead men with fire; nor is it lawful to bury them in the earth and heap a mound above them, but they must be wrapped in untanned ox-hides and hung from trees far from the city. Yet earth has an equal share of fate with air, since they bury their women in the ground — for such is the ordinance established by custom.

As they made their way, Hera in her kindness spread a thick mist through the city on their behalf, so that they might pass unseen by the countless Colchian people as they went to Aeetes' palace. But as soon as they had come from the plain into the city and the halls of Aeetes, Hera then dispersed the cloud again. They stood in the forecourt, marveling at the king's enclosure, the wide gates and columns rising in a row around the walls; and above the palace a cornice of stone was fitted upon bronze carvings. Quietly they then crossed the threshold. Close by, grapevines covered with green leaves towered high and flourished greatly. Beneath them four ever-flowing springs ran, which Hephaestus had fashioned: one welled up with milk, one with wine, the third flowed with fragrant oil, and the fourth sent forth water — water that grew warm when the Pleiades were setting, and then as they rose again bubbled up from the hollow rock cold as crystal. Such were the marvelous works that the cunning Hephaestus had contrived in the palace of Aeetes of Cytaea. And he had made for him bulls with hooves of bronze, and their

[The bulls'] mouths breathed out a terrible blast of fire, and Aeetes had driven up also a sturdy plow of unyielding adamant, in return for a favor to Helios, who had received him on his horses when exhausted from the battle of Phlegra.

There too was built a courtyard in the middle, and upon it were many well-fitted double doors opening to chambers here and there. A richly wrought portico ran along either side, and at an angle on both sides stood taller buildings. In one of these, the foremost in dignity, dwelt the lord Aeetes with his wife; in another Apsyrtus, the son of Aeetes, whom a Caucasian nymph, Asterodeia, had borne him before he took Eidyia, daughter of Tethys and Oceanus — the youngest of their children — as his wedded wife. And the sons of the Colchians called him by the surname Phaethon, because he outshone all the young men. These two daughters of Aeetes, along with their attendants, were in his company — Chalciope and Medea. The latter was on her way from her chamber to her sister's room — for Hera kept her at home, and she had not been in the habit of frequenting the palace before, but spent her days at the temple of Hecate, since she was herself the goddess's priestess. When she saw them drawing near she cried out, and Chalciope heard her clearly. The handmaidens, dropping their yarn and spindles at their feet, all rushed outside together. And Chalciope, seeing her own sons among them, raised her hands aloft in joy; and they likewise greeted their mother and embraced her gladly at the sight; and weeping, she spoke these words:

'Yet they were not destined to wander far, leaving me without care — fate turned them back to you. Wretched me! What a longing for Greece they took upon themselves from afar, through the ruinous infatuation kindled by the dying commands of Phrixus our father. He, as he died, laid bitter griefs upon our hearts. But why should you have come to the city of Orchomenus — whoever this Orchomenus may be — for the sake of Athamas's wealth, abandoning your own mother in her grief?'

So she spoke. Last of all, Aeetes rose and went out through the door, and after him went Eidyia herself, the wife of Aeetes, when she heard Chalciope's name. At once the whole courtyard was filled with noise. Some of the servants were busying themselves around a great bull, others were chopping dry logs with bronze axes, others heating water over fire for bathing; and there was no one who relaxed from his toil, serving the king.

Meanwhile Eros came unseen through the grey air, turbulent as the gadfly that drives young heifers mad — the one the herdsmen call the breeze-fly. Quickly, beneath the porch, under the entrance-hall, he strung his bow, and drew from his quiver an arrow never yet shot, one that brings much sorrow. He darted swiftly across the threshold with quick feet, unnoticed, glancing sharply about. Crouching low beside Jason, he fitted the notch of the arrow to the middle of the string, and drawing it back with both hands let it fly at Medea. A speechless stupor seized her heart. Eros himself, laughing, sped back out of the high-roofed hall. The arrow burned deep within the girl, beneath her heart, like a flame. She kept throwing glances at Jason, and her breath came

From his chest his crowded wits were worn with toil, and he had no thought of anything else; his spirit was melting away with sweet pain. As a poor working woman heaps dry sticks around a burning brand — one for whom spinning is her constant care — so that she may kindle a light beneath her roof during the night, waking very early; and the flame, fed from that small brand, blazes up and burns all the sticks together: so Eros, destructive, crept beneath her heart and burned there in secret, and her soft cheeks shifted from pale to red, in the distraction of her mind.

When the servants had set out a ready meal for them, and they themselves had refreshed their bodies in warm baths, they gladly cheered their hearts with food and drink. Then Aeetes questioned the sons of his daughter and of Phrixus, whom above all strangers he had honored in his halls, encouraging them with these words:

"Sons of my daughter and of Phrixus, whom I honored above all strangers in my palace — how is it that you have come back to Aea so swiftly? Did some disaster break you midway as you made your escape? You would not listen when I told you the boundless measure of the journey. For I myself once knew it, riding in my father Helios's chariot, when he was bringing my sister Circe to the land of the West, and we came to the shore of the Tyrrhenian mainland, where she still lives to this day, very far indeed from Colchian soil. But why dwell on stories? Tell me plainly what has happened before you here, and who these men are who accompany you, and from where you disembarked from your hollow ship."

So he questioned them, and before his nephews Argos, fearing for the expedition of Aeson's son, addressed him gently, since he was the eldest:

"Aeetes, that ship was quickly scattered by violent storms, and the waves cast them, fallen beneath the timbers, onto the dry shore of the island of Enyalius in grim darkness; but some god saved us. For we did not find the Ares-birds that used to nest on that desolate island before — those men had driven them away, having disembarked from their own ship the day before. And the mind of Zeus, pitying us, or some fate, held them back, so that straightaway they gave us food in plenty and clothing, and heard the famous name of Phrixus and of yourself; for they are sailing to your city. And the need, if you wish to know it, I will not hide from you. A certain king, eager to drive this man far from his homeland and his possessions — because he excelled all the sons of Aeolus in his own prowess — has sent him here on an impossible mission; and he declares he will not escape the heart-piercing wrath and anger of unyielding Zeus, nor the dreadful guilt, nor the retribution owed to the race of the Aeolids for Phrixus, before the fleece reaches Hellas. The ship Pallas Athena built — nothing like the ships the Colchian men have, the worst of which we encountered; for violent water and wind tear such apart — but ours is held fast by its bolts even when all the storms bear down upon it. It runs equally well driven by the wind or when the men themselves press hard upon the oars with steady hands. On it he has gathered the best of the heroes of all Achaea and has come to your city, having wandered over many towns and the seas of the hateful salt, in hopes that you might grant him the fleece."

"It shall be as he wishes; for he comes not to press his claim by force. He intends to pay you worthy recompense for your gift, by subduing the Sauromatae, who are a great menace to you, and will bring them under your scepter.

But if you desire to learn their names and lineage, I will tell you everything. This man, on whose account the rest gathered from Hellas, is called Jason, son of Aeson, son of Cretheus. And if he truly is of Cretheus' own blood, he would be our kinsman on the father's side. For both Cretheus and Athamas were sons of Aeolus, and Phrixus was the son of Athamas, himself of Aeolus' line. And this man here — if you have heard that any son of Helios lives — you behold Augeas. And this is Telamon, sprung from most glorious Aeacus; and Zeus himself begat Aeacus. And so too all the others who follow as companions are sons and grandsons of immortals."

Such were the words Argus spoke. But the king, as he listened, was enraged by what was said, and his heart swelled high with anger. He burst out furiously, and his wrath was aimed above all at the sons of Chalciope, for he suspected that it was on their account that the strangers had come. His eyes blazed out from beneath his brows in his fury:

"Get out of my sight at once, you scoundrels, and take your schemes with you — out of this land — before someone sees to his sorrow both the fleece and Phrixus! You have come here together from Hellas not for the fleece, but to seize my scepter and my royal power. If you had not already touched my table as guests,

218

— she who would have cut out your tongues and lopped off both your hands and sent you away on the feet I gave you, so that you might be stopped from going further; and such lies you told to the blessed gods.'

So he spoke in his rage; and the heart of Aeacus's grandson swelled with fury from within; and his spirit yearned to hurl back a deadly word of defiance. But the son of Aeson held him back, for he himself stepped forward and replied with gentle words:

'Aeetes, bear with us on this voyage. For it is not as you perhaps suppose that we have come to your city and your halls, nor were we driven by desire for them. Who would willingly cross so vast a sea to seize another's treasure? No — a god and the cruel command of a reckless king drove me here. Grant this favor to those who ask it; and I will carry your glorious fame through all of Greece. And we are already ready to repay you swiftly with service in war, whether you desire to subdue the Sauromatae or any other people under your scepter.'

So he spoke, winning him over with gentle voice; but the king's heart churned with two competing impulses: whether to rush upon them and cut them down on the spot, or to put their strength to the test. This second course seemed better to him as he weighed it; and he answered them in reply:

'Stranger, why should you recount each detail at length? If you are truly of divine descent, or at least no worse than I, and have come among strangers on such a quest, I will give you the golden fleece to take away, if you are willing to make trial of yourself. For against men of valor I bear no grudge, as you yourselves declare of the one who rules over Greece.

A trial of your courage and strength shall the contest be — one which I myself handle with my own hands, deadly though it is. Two bronze-footed bulls graze for me on the plain of Ares, breathing flame from their mouths; I drive them and yoke them over the hard fallow of Ares, four acres of it, and quickly cutting it to the headland with the plow, I sow in the furrows not Demeter's grain, but the teeth of a terrible serpent, which spring up as armed men; these I then mow down as they rise and press around me, slaying them with my spear. I yoke the bulls at dawn and stop my harvesting at the evening hour. You, if you accomplish such tasks as these, shall carry off the fleece that very day to your king's hall. Before that I will not give it — do not expect it. For it is surely shameful that a man of good birth should yield to one of lesser worth.'

So he spoke; and Jason fixed his eyes on the ground before his feet and sat there speechless, helpless in his distress. For a long time he turned the matter over in his mind, with no way to accept the challenge boldly, since the task seemed immense. But at last he replied and addressed him with cunning words:

'Aeëtes, you constrain me altogether with strict justice. Therefore I will undertake the contest, monstrous as it is, even if it is my fate to die. For nothing worse can press upon mortals than bitter necessity — and it is that which drove me to come here at a king's command.'

So he spoke, struck with helplessness; but Aeëtes addressed him in his distress with terrible words:

"Go now among the throng, since you are eager for the labor. But if you shrink from yoking the bulls or from reaping the deadly crop, then all this shall be my concern, so that another man too may shudder to seek out a better champion."

So he spoke bluntly. And Jason rose from his seat, and with him Augeas and Telamon close by; Argos alone followed, for he had signaled his brothers to remain there in the hall. So they went out from the palace.

Among them all, the son of Aeson stood out surpassingly in beauty and grace. And the maiden gazed at him sidelong, holding her shining veil aside, her heart smoldering with grief; and her mind, like a dream, crept after his retreating steps.

So they departed from the hall with troubled hearts. But Chalciope, wary of Aeetes' anger, had already gone quickly to her chamber with her sons. Medea likewise withdrew; and in her heart she turned over many things, all that the Loves urge one to dwell upon. Still before her eyes everything lingered — his very look, what garments he wore, what he said, how he sat upon his seat, and how he walked to the door. As she brooded, she could imagine no other man his equal. In her ears his voice and his honeyed words forever rang, the words he had spoken. She feared for him, lest the bulls or Aeetes himself might destroy him; and she mourned as though he were already utterly dead, and around her tender cheeks tears flowed in deepest pity and grief. And softly, weeping, she breathed forth these words:

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

'Why does this grief hold me, poor wretch? Whether he perishes as the best of heroes or the worst, let him go. Yet would that he had escaped unharmed. Yes, let this come to pass, O queenly goddess Persephone, that he return home escaping his doom; but if it is his fate to be overcome by the bulls, let him learn that first, so that I do not rejoice over him in his evil ruin.'

So the maiden's mind was troubled by these anxious thoughts. But when the others had gone out beyond the people and the city along the road by which they had come up from the plain, then Argos addressed Jason with these words:

'Son of Aeson, you will find fault with the plan I am about to propose, yet in our trouble it does not seem right to give up trying. You have heard from me before of a certain girl who practices magic under the instruction of Hecate, daughter of Perses. If we could win her over, I think there would no longer be any fear of your being overcome in the contest; but I greatly dread that my mother may not agree to this. Nevertheless I will go back again and entreat her, for destruction hangs over all of us alike.'

So he spoke with good intent, and Jason answered him with these words: 'My friend, if this seems good to you, I have no objection. Go, and rouse your mother with persuasive words to help us; though indeed a pitiful hope is ours, when we have entrusted our return to women.'

So he spoke, and quickly they came back to the marsh. And their companions questioned them joyfully when they saw them approaching; and the son of Aeson, heavy-hearted, spoke to them:

226

"Friends, the cruel heart of Aeetes is bitterly enraged against us; there is no point in deliberating every detail — it would get us nowhere, neither for me nor for you in your debating. He declared that two bulls with bronze hooves graze the Arian plain, breathing flame from their mouths. He commanded that a four-acre field be ploughed with them; and he will give seed from the serpent's jaws, which springs up as earth-born warriors in bronze armor — and these must be destroyed on that very same day. I accepted his challenge outright — for there was no better course to take."

So he spoke; and to all of them the task seemed impossible. For a long time they stood in silence, staring at one another, downcast with helplessness and despair. At last Peleus spoke up boldly among all the chieftains:

"Now is the time to decide what we will do. I do not think counsel is as valuable as the strength of our hands. If you, hero son of Aeson, are resolved to yoke Aeetes' bulls and are eager for the labor, then keep your promise and make your preparations. But if your spirit does not fully trust your own strength, then neither press yourself forward nor look around among these men while you sit idle. For I myself will not hold back — since death will be the most painful outcome."

So spoke the son of Aeacus. The heart of Telamon was stirred; he leaped up eagerly and swiftly. Third rose Idas, full of pride; and after him the twin sons of Tyndareus; and with them Oeneus' son, counted among the company of fighting men, not yet so much as showing the first down upon his cheeks —

— rising up; such was the courage swelling in him with its might. The others yielded and kept silent. Straightaway Argus addressed them with these words, as they were eager for the contest:

"Friends, this is indeed our last resort. But I think there will yet come to you a fitting help from my mother. Therefore, eager as you are, hold back a little longer in the ship, as before — for it is better to restrain ourselves nonetheless than to choose a terrible fate by throwing caution to the winds. There is a maiden reared in the halls of Aeetes, whom the goddess Hecate taught above all others to work with drugs, whatever the land produces and the flowing waters. With these she soothes even the blast of tireless fire, and swiftly stops rivers as they rush roaring down, and has bound the paths of the stars and the sacred moon. Going from her palace along the path here, we remembered, if she could — she being our sister — to persuade our mother to assist us in the contest. And if this also seems good to you yourselves, I could go this very day back to the house of Aeetes to make the attempt; and perhaps with the favor of heaven the attempt may succeed."

So he spoke. And the gods, being gracious, gave them a sign. A trembling dove fleeing the force of a hawk fell in her terror from above into the lap of Jason; and the hawk crashed down upon the stern-ornament. Quickly Mopsus spoke among them all with these prophetic words:

"Friends, this sign has been shaped by the will of the gods, and there is no better way to interpret it: we must approach the maiden and attend to her with every kind of persuasion. And I think she will not spurn us,

— if truly Phineus declared to the goddess Cypris that a homecoming
was to be. Her gentle bird escaped its destined fate; and as my heart
perceives this omen, so may it come to pass.
Come, friends, invoking Cytherea to aid us,
obey now the counsels of Argus.'

So he spoke; and the young men approved, remembering the commands of Phineus. But alone among them, Idas son of Aphareus leapt up,
raging terribly, and cried out in a great voice:
'Oh, what a disgrace — have we come here as companions to women,
calling on Cypris to be our helper,
no longer trusting in the great might of Enyalius? And do you hold back from contests by watching doves and hawks?
Away with you — let no thought of warlike deeds concern you,
but go and win over helpless girls with flattering prayers.'

So he spoke in his fury; and many of his companions murmured
very softly, and none spoke a word against him.
Seething with anger, he sat back down; and Jason,
at once stirring his own resolve, spoke thus among them:
'Since this plan has pleased everyone, let Argus set out from the ship;
but we ourselves will openly make fast the cables
from the river to the shore. For truly it seems fitting
no longer to hide ourselves in cowering fear of her.'

So he spoke; and immediately he sent Argus ahead to go
swiftly back into the city; while the others, at the command of the son of Aeson,
drew the mooring-stones of the ship and rowed it
a little way out of the marsh onto dry land.

Straightaway Aeetes held an assembly of the Colchians
apart from his palace, in the place where they had sat before,
devising unbearable treacheries and troubles for the Minyans.
He vowed that, once the bulls had first done their destructive work —

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK III

Phineus said that our return would be aided by the Cyprian goddess. It was her gentle bird that escaped death; and just as my heart within me foresees in accordance with this omen, so may it come true! But, my friends, let us call on Cytherea to help us, and immediately follow the advice of Argus."

He spoke, and the warriors agreed, remembering the instructions of Phineus; but Idas, son of Aphareus, leapt up alone and shouted loudly in terrible fury: "Shame on us — have we come here as fellow voyagers with women, calling on Cypris for help rather than on the mighty strength of Enyalius? And do you look to doves and hawks to save yourselves from battle? Away with you — think not of deeds of war, but rather use prayer to win over weak girls."

Those were his heated words; and many of his comrades murmured quietly, but not one spoke a word in reply. He sat back down in anger; and at once Jason rallied them and spoke his own mind: "Let Argus go back from the ship, since this is what we have all agreed; but now we will move away from the river and openly tie our mooring ropes to the shore. For it is surely no longer right for us to remain hiding and cowering from the battle-cry."

With that he spoke, and immediately sent Argus hurrying back to the city; and they hauled up the anchors at the command of Aeson's son, and rowed the ship close to the shore, a short distance from the backwater.

But right away Aeetes held an assembly of the Colchians, far from his palace at a place where they had gathered in earlier times, to plot grim treachery and trouble against the Minyae. And he threatened

the man who had agreed to accomplish a heavy labor — to split open the forest above the wooded hill and burn the ship together with its crew, so that those who plotted overweening deeds might flee from their dreadful outrage. For not even the son of Aeolus, Phrixus, much as he needed it, had he received as a guest at his hearth — though Phrixus surpassed all strangers in gentleness and reverence for the gods — unless Zeus himself had sent Hermes down from heaven so that he might meet him as a kinsman; lest the pirates who came into his land should long remain unharmed, men whose concern it is to lift their hands against others' property, to devise secret treacheries, and to raid the sheepfolds of herdsmen with clamorous attacks. And apart from that, he said that the sons of Phrixus would bring fitting recompense upon him personally — companions of wicked men returning home in a band — so that without care they might drive him from his honor and his scepter; just as he had once heard the ominous prophecy of his father Helios, that need and cunning deceit and the plans of his own offspring and their ruinous scheming would bring about his undoing. Therefore he was sending them willingly to the Achaean land at their father's command, on a long journey. He had no great fear of his daughters devising some dreadful plan, nor of his son Absyrtus; but in the family of Chalciope these dire things had come to pass. And he in his rage was denouncing these unbearable deeds to the people, and loudly threatened them: to haul the ship up onto land and keep the men there, so that not one might escape his punishment.

Meanwhile, as he made his way to the palace of Aeetes, Argos kept trying to persuade his mother with every kind of argument to beg Medea to help them. She herself had already been thinking of it, but fear held back her heart — fear that she might be pleading in vain against her father's terrible rage, which would only drive him to greater fury, or that if she yielded to their prayers, her deeds would become plain and open for all to see.

Then sweet sleep released the girl from her sorrows as she lay back on her bed. But at once, treacherous and tormenting dreams — as was fitting for one so distressed — began to haunt her. She dreamed that the stranger had taken on the contest, not at all with the aim of carrying off the fleece of the ram, nor was that the reason he had come to the city of Aeetes — but so that he might bring her home as his lawful wife. And she dreamed that she herself was pitting her strength against the bulls with great ease; but that her own parents were going back on their promise, since the task had been set not for their daughter but for the stranger himself. From this there arose a bitter quarrel between her father and the strangers; and both sides left the decision to her, to settle as her own heart might direct. Then she suddenly chose the stranger, with no regard for her parents. Grief beyond bearing seized them and they cried out in anger. At their cry, sleep released her. She leapt up trembling with fright and looked all around the walls of her chamber. Barely she gathered her wits back into her breast as before, and let out a heartfelt cry:

"Poor wretch that I am — how these heavy dreams have frightened me! I fear that this journey of his will bring some great evil.

of heroes. My mind is stirred on behalf of a stranger. Let him seek far away in his own land his Achaean girl; let maidenhood and the house of my parents be my concern. Yet, steeling my heart to shamelessness, I will no longer hold back from my sister, to see if she will meet me with help for the contest, grieving as she does for her own children — that might quench the bitter pain in my heart.'

So she spoke, and rising up she opened the doors of her chamber, barefoot and wearing only her robe. She was eager to go to her sister and had already crossed the threshold of the court. But she lingered there a long time in the entrance hall of her chamber, held back by shame; then she turned and went back inside, and again came forth, and again shrank back in — her feet carried her aimlessly here and there; whenever she pressed forward, shame held her back from within; but as shame restrained her, bold desire urged her on. Three times she tried, three times she stopped, and a fourth time she fell forward onto her bed, curling up.

As when a young bride mourns for her tender husband in her chamber — the one to whom her brothers and parents have given her — and she does not yet mingle with all her attendants out of modesty and thoughtfulness, but sits grieving in the inner room; some fate has destroyed him before they could both take joy in each other's love; and she, though burning inwardly, weeps in silence gazing at her widowed bed, lest the women mock and taunt her — just like her did Medea weep. But suddenly one of her attendants, coming in upon her, noticed her in the midst of her lamenting,

of the handmaids, who had been her attendant since girlhood.
Chalciope brought her the news straightway; and she was sitting among her children,
devising how to win over her sister.
But she did not disobey even so, when she heard from her attendant
the unexpected message; and she rushed in amazement          670
straight through from chamber to chamber, where the girl
lay sorrowing, and tore both her cheeks.
And when she saw her eyes all wet with tears, she said to her:
"Ah, woe is me, Medea! Why do you shed these tears?
What has happened to you? What terrible grief has come upon your heart?
Has some divinely-sent disease run through your limbs,
or have you heard some dreadful rebuke from our father
concerning me and my children? Would that I had never looked upon
this house of my parents, nor upon this city, but lived at the ends
of the earth, where not even the name of Colchians is known."     680
So she spoke; and the girl's cheeks flushed red, and for a long time
maiden shame held her back from answering, eager as she was.
The words kept rising now to the tip of her tongue,
now falling back again deep in her breast.
Often they surged sweetly to her lips, longing to be spoken,
but went no further in sound; at last she said this with guile,
for the bold Loves were urging her on:
"Chalciope, my heart is trembling for your sons,
lest their father destroy them at once together with the foreign men.
Such grim dreams I behold, just roused from brief sleep,          690
dreams which some god may render without fulfillment,
so that you need not take upon yourself grievous sorrow for your sons."

She spoke, testing her sister, to see if she herself might come before her and plead for the sake of her sons. A terrible, unbearable grief flooded Medea's heart at what she heard, and she answered her with these words:

'I too have come here turning all these things over in my mind, to see if you might devise some plan and provide help. But swear by Earth and Heaven that what I tell you you will keep in your heart, and that you will join with me as my helper. I beg you by the blessed gods and by yourself and your parents: do not let me see them torn apart by an evil fate in misery—or else, if I die together with your dear children, may I be a hateful Fury to you from Hades hereafter.'

So she spoke, and immediately a great flood of tears burst forth; she clasped her knees below with both hands and laid her head upon her bosom. Then piteously they both broke into lamentation over each other, and a thin wail rose through the halls with the sounds of their grieving. Medea spoke to her first, in her distress:

'Wretch that I am, what cure can I provide for you, as you speak of dreadful curses and Furies? Would that they truly existed to guard your sons among us! Let the great oath of the Colchians, by which you urge me to swear—mighty Heaven above, or Earth below, mother of the gods—bear witness: so far as my power extends, you shall not lack whatever can be accomplished in helping you.'

So she said, and Chalciope answered her with these words:

'Could you not then find it in your heart to devise some trick, or some scheme regarding the contest, for the stranger who is himself in need, for the sake of my children? And from him there comes—

Argos, urging me to try to win your help; and him I left behind in the palace as I came here.'

So she spoke; and within her, the heart leapt up with joy, and all at once her lovely skin flushed red, and a mist came over her as she melted with warmth, and she spoke to her these words:

'Chalciope, as you and yours hold dear and precious, so will I act. For may the dawn never shine before my eyes, nor may you look upon me living much longer, if I were to place anything above your life or above your children, who are to me as brothers, beloved and dear companions and of the same age. And I claim likewise to be both your sister and the daughter of the same parents, since just as them, you nursed me at your breast when I was a babe, as I always used to hear from my mother. But go, and conceal my kindness in silence, so that I may prepare the fulfillment of my promise without my parents knowing. At dawn I will go to the temple of Hecate and bring the drugs that charm bulls.'

So she spoke and led her back out of the chamber, and told her children of the help their own sister would give. Then shame and dread gripped Medea again as she was left alone, at what she was devising against her own father's wishes for a man's sake.

Then night brought darkness over the earth, and out on the sea sailors looked up from their ships to Helice and the stars of Orion; and now the traveler and the gate-keeper longed for sleep; and a deep slumber wrapped around a mother whose children had died.

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

No longer was there the barking of dogs throughout the city, no resounding noise; silence held the darkening night. But sweet sleep did not come upon Medea. For many anxieties kept her wakeful in her longing for Jason, fearing the mighty strength of the bulls, by which he was fated to perish by an unseemly fate in the field of Ares. Thick and fast her heart throbbed within her breast, as a sunbeam dances through a house, reflected from water which has just been poured into a cauldron or perhaps into a pail; and as it quivers this way and that in the swift eddy, so the girl's heart trembled within her breast. Tears flowed from her eyes in pity; and within her, a pain smoldered ceaselessly through her flesh, winding around the fine nerves and deep beneath the base of the skull, where the sharpest anguish enters whenever the tireless Loves drive their pains into the mind. Now she thought she would give him the enchanting drugs for the bulls, now she would not; then that she herself would perish; then again that she would neither die herself nor give the drugs, but calmly endure her misfortune as it was. Then she sat down and wavered in her mind, and spoke: "Wretched that I am — where shall I turn now, to this side of my troubles or to that? On every side my wits are helpless; there is no remedy for my pain; it burns on without cease. Would that I had been struck down first by the swift arrows of Artemis, before I saw him, before the sons of Chalciope came to the Achaean land. Some god or some Fury brought them here from there, to our great grief and weeping. Let him perish in the contest, if it is his fate to die in the field —"

such is my fate. For how could I conceal from my parents what I have plotted with my drugs? What story could I tell them? What trick, what cunning scheme could bring him aid? Should I approach him alone, apart from his companions, when I see him? I am wretched — I have no hope that even after his death I shall find any relief from my grief; then would evil come upon us, when he is torn from life. Let shame go, let reputation go — and may he, saved by my help and unharmed, go wherever his heart desires. As for me, on that very day when he completes his task, let me die — either hanging my neck from a rafter, or taking a draught of drugs that destroy life. Yet even so, after my death they will mock me behind my back; and the whole city far and wide will cry out at my fate, and the Colchian women, passing me from mouth to mouth, will everywhere revile me shamefully — she who cared so much for a foreign man that she died, she who brought shame upon her home and her parents, yielding to her madness. What disgrace will not be mine? Ah, what ruin is my own! Far better it would be this very night to leave life here in my chamber by an unlooked-for fate, escaping all reproach, before I bring these shameful and unspeakable things to pass.'

So she spoke, and went to fetch a casket in which lay many drugs of hers, some healing and some deadly. She set it on her knees and wept. She drenched her robe ceaselessly with tears that fell in streams, weeping bitterly over her own fate. She was eager to take out the life-destroying drugs and swallow them. Already she was undoing the fastenings of the casket, in her eagerness to take them out — poor wretch. But suddenly

The dreadful fear of loathsome Hades came upon her heart. For a long time she was held speechless, and all the cherished cares of life crowded around her mind. She thought of all the joys that belong to the living, she thought of the glad companions of her youth, as a girl does; and the sun grew sweeter to look upon than before, if indeed she had truly reflected on each thing in her mind. Then, in accordance with Hera's promptings, she changed her resolve and set aside her plan, putting it back upon her knees, no longer wavering between two counsels; she longed eagerly for the dawn to appear so that she might give him the charmed drugs as they had agreed, and meet him face to face. Often she would undo the bolts of her doors, watching for the gleam of light; and welcome indeed did the morning star shed its brightness for her, and throughout the city everyone began to stir.

Then Argos bade his brothers remain there while he went to learn the maiden's mind and her intentions; he himself went on ahead back to the ship.

And when the young girl first saw the dawn breaking, she took her golden hair in her hands — it had been hanging loose and unkempt — and smoothed her tear-dried cheeks, and anointed her skin with fragrant nectar-oil, and put on a beautiful robe fastened with well-curved brooches, and upon her immortal head she cast a shining silver veil. And there within her rooms she paced the floor, forgetting her sorrows — those already at her feet and those that were yet to grow greater in time to come. She called to her handmaids, all twelve of them, who slept in the vestibule of her fragrant chamber,

peers of her age, girls not yet acquainted with the marriage bed, who speedily yoked the mules to the wagon, so that they might bring her to the beautiful temple of Hecate. Meanwhile the handmaids were making ready the wagon, and Medea took from the hollow chest a drug which men call the Promethean herb.

If a man were to propitiate the Maiden alone-begotten with night-offerings and anoint his body with this drug, he would be invulnerable to the stroke of bronze and would not yield to burning fire; but for that day he would prove superior alike in strength and valor.

It had first sprung up where the blood-like ichor of the suffering Prometheus dripped to the ground from the talons of the eagle on the Caucasian rocks. Its flower bloomed to the height of a cubit above ground, in color like the Corycian crocus, rising on twin stalks; but in the earth the root was like newly cut flesh.

The dark juice of this root, like the sap of a mountain oak, she had gathered in a Caspian shell to prepare her charm, having first bathed in seven ever-flowing streams, and having called seven times on Brimo, nurse of youth — Brimo, wanderer of the night, of the underworld, queen of the dead — in the darkness of night, clad in shadowy garments.

The black earth groaned and rumbled beneath her as the Titan root was severed, and the son of Iapetus himself groaned, his spirit distressed with pain.

Medea took out the drug and placed it in the fragrant band that was fastened about her ambrosial breast. Then she went out and mounted the swift wagon, and two of her handmaids mounted on either side of her.

She herself took the reins and the well-made whip in her right hand, and drove through the city; and the other handmaids, grasping the rail of the car behind, ran along the broad wagon road, and lifted their thin tunics up to the white knee. As Leto's daughter, standing on her golden chariot drawn by swift deer, speeds over the hills after bathing in the warm waters of Parthenios or Amnisus, coming from afar to meet a rich-scented hecatomb — 880 and with her the nymphs attend in a troop, some gathered from the very spring of Amnisus, others from the groves and the many-fountained heights; and around her beasts fawn and whimper, trembling as she passes — just so they sped through the city; and the people made way on either side, avoiding the eyes of the royal maiden. But when she had left the well-built streets of the city behind and, driving across the plain, had reached the temple, she stepped down then and there from the smooth-rolling car, and spoke thus to her handmaids: 890 "Friends, truly I have committed a great fault, and did not think to prevent the going among foreign men who wander over our land. Helplessness has seized the whole city; not one of those women who used to gather here day by day has come. But since we have arrived and no one else will come, let us freely satisfy our hearts with gentle song, and gathering the fair flowers of the tender grass, let us then return home at the proper hour."

And you would return home with abundant gifts on that very day, if you agree to this plan I have in mind. For Argos is urging me with his words, and so too is Chalciope herself; but keep what you hear from me in silence in your hearts, lest my father's ears catch wind of it. They are asking me — since a stranger has undertaken the trial of the bulls — to save him from the deadly contests in exchange for gifts. I approved of the plan, and I have summoned him to come alone, away from his companions, so that we may share the gifts among ourselves, if he brings them; but to him in turn we will provide another, more deadly charm. But stand apart from me when he arrives.'

So she spoke, and the crafty scheme pleased them all. Then straightaway Argos drew Jason aside from his companions — for he had already heard that Medea was going at dawn toward the sacred temple of Hecate — and led him across the plain; and with them went Mopsus son of Ampycus, skilled at reading the omens of birds that appeared before them, and skilled at deliberating wisely on the way.

Never before among men of earlier times had there been anyone like this — not among those who were of the lineage of Zeus himself, nor among the heroes who had sprung from the blood of the other immortals — as the wife of Zeus made Jason on that day, both to look upon and to speak with. Even his own companions gazed at him in amazement as he shone with grace; and Mopsus son of Ampycus rejoiced at their going, already divining how everything would turn out.

There is along the path of the plain, near the temple, a poplar tree clothed in countless leaves; in it noisy crows were accustomed to roost in flocks.

One of them, moving her wings through the air midway among the high branches, declared the counsels of Hera:
"This seer is without glory, who cannot grasp even what children know — for neither a sweet nor a loving word would a girl speak to a young man when strangers are at hand. Away with you, wretched prophet, fool! Neither Cypris nor the gentle, loving Erotes breathe upon you."

So she spoke in reproach; but Mopsus smiled when he heard the god-sent voice of the bird, and spoke thus:
"You yourself go to the temple of the goddess — there you will find the maiden, son of Aeson. You will meet with her very graciously by the favor of Cypris, who will be your ally in the contests, as Phineus, son of Agenor, foretold before. As for us two — myself and Argos — we will wait for you here in this very spot when you return. Go alone, and win her over with words of shrewd persuasion."

He spoke with good judgment, and both of the others approved. Nor could Medea's heart turn to think of other things, though she went on singing; for every song she played did not long please her to perform. She kept breaking off, distracted, and could never keep her eyes steadily on the crowd of her handmaids — she kept glancing far along the paths, turning her cheek aside. Many a time her heart broke in her breast when she thought she heard the thud of a footstep or the rush of the wind. But before long he appeared to her longing eyes, rising up on high like Sirius from the ocean — that star which rises beautiful and radiant to behold, yet brings unspeakable misery to the flocks. So to her he came, beautiful to look upon — the son of Aeson — but appearing thus, he stirred in her a painful, wretched longing.

And at once her heart fell from her breast, and her eyes likewise grew dim. A warm flush took hold of her cheeks. She had no strength to lift her knees, either backward or forward, but her feet were rooted to the ground beneath her. Meanwhile all her handmaidens had drawn aside from them. So the two stood facing one another, speechless and without a word, like oaks or tall firs that stand rooted quietly in the mountains in calm weather, but then stir and murmur without end when the wind's blast comes upon them. Just so were those two about to speak at length under the breath of Love. Jason, the son of Aeson, perceived that she had fallen into a heaven-sent bewilderment, and spoke to her in soothing words:

"Why do you fear me so, maiden, seeing what manner of man I am? I am not, as other men are who are arrogant boasters — not even when I lived in my own homeland was I such before. Therefore do not be overly bashful before me, girl, whether you wish to ask something dear to you or to say something. Since we have come to one another in goodwill, in this sacred place where it is not lawful to do wrong, speak openly and ask freely. Do not deceive me with honeyed words, since from the first you promised your own sister that you would give the charms she needs. I implore you by Hecate herself and by your parents and by Zeus, who holds his hand over strangers and suppliants alike — for I come to you here as both suppliant and stranger, brought by pressing need, and kneeling before you. Without your help I shall not overcome the grievous trial. In return, I will repay you hereafter for your aid, as is right and fitting, since we dwell in lands far apart from one another.

...winning a name and fine glory; and just as other heroes will call upon you when they return to Greece, and the wives and mothers of heroes, who even now perhaps sit on the shore and wail for us — you could scatter their bitter grief.

Once before, the maiden daughter of Minos, Ariadne, kindly-spirited, freed Theseus from terrible trials — she whom Pasiphae, daughter of the Sun, had borne. And when Minos had stilled his anger, she left her homeland aboard ship with him; the immortals themselves loved her, and as a sign for her in the midst of the sky, a crown of stars, which men call Ariadne's crown, wheels all night long among the heavenly constellations. So too shall divine favor come to you, if you save so great a company of heroic men. For from your appearance you seem suited to gentle grace and courtesy.'

So he spoke, honoring her with praise. She cast her eyes down with a gentle sidelong glance and smiled a smile like nectar; her heart melted within her, lifted by his flattery, and she looked up to meet his gaze directly. She had no idea what words to speak first, but longed to pour out everything at once. With no hesitation she drew the charm from her fragrant sash, and he took it in his hands with joy.

She would have drawn out her whole soul from her breast and given it, so enraptured was she by his need — such was the sweet flame that Eros flashed from the golden head of the son of Aeson, and it stole the brightness of her eyes; and within, her heart melted as she grew warm, just as dew on roses melts, warmed by the morning light.

Both of them at times fixed their eyes on the ground in shame, and at other times cast glances at each other, smiling with longing beneath their bright brows. At last the girl barely managed to address them with these words:

'Listen now, so that I may devise help for you. When my father gives you the deadly teeth from the serpent's jaws to sow, then watch for the mid-point of night, and after bathing in the streams of the tireless river, alone, apart from the others, clad in dark robes, dig a round pit; over it slaughter a female lamb and burn it whole, piling up the pyre well over the pit itself. Then propitiate Hecate, the only-begotten daughter of Persia, pouring from a cup the honeyed labor of bees. And when you have remembered to appease the goddess, step back from the pyre; and do not let the sound of feet make you turn to look back, nor the barking of dogs, lest you ruin everything and fail to return in proper order to your comrades. In the morning, soaking this charm and anointing your bare body with it as with oil, you will find in it boundless strength and great power, and you would say you were matched not with men but with the immortal gods. And let your spear be sprinkled with it as well, and your shield and sword. Then the points of the earth-born men will not pierce you, nor the irresistible rushing flame of the savage bulls. Yet you will not remain so for long — only for that one day. Nevertheless, do not ever shrink from the contest. And I will give you yet another aid besides: when you have yoked the mighty bulls and have quickly plowed with your hands and strength through all the hard fallow field,

Already along the furrows the Giants were sprouting up from the sown serpent's teeth upon the dark clods of earth. If you see many of them rising up from the ploughland, throw a heavy stone among them secretly; and they, like fierce dogs fighting over food, will destroy one another; then press forward yourself eager for battle. In this way you will carry the fleece to Hellas from Aia far away; yet go wherever you wish, wherever it pleased you to sail when you set out.'

So she spoke, and casting her eyes silently to the ground before his feet, she wet her divine cheeks with warm tears, lamenting that he was about to wander far away over the wide sea far from her. Again she addressed him with a sorrowful word, and took him by the right hand; for by now shame had left her eyes:

'Remember, if ever you return home, the name of Medea; and I in turn will remember you even when you are far away. But tell me willingly this: where are your home and halls, where will you sail from here over the sea? Will you come near wealthy Orchomenus, or near the island of Aeaea? And tell me of the girl, whoever she is, that you mentioned, the famous daughter of Pasiphae, who is a kinswoman of my father.'

So she spoke; and over him too cruel Eros sent the tears of the girl, and he answered her with these words in reply:

'Truly I think I shall never forget you, neither by night nor by day, if I truly escape death and flee safely to Achaea, and Aeetes sets us no worse task than this to accomplish.

"And if it pleases you to learn of my homeland, I will tell you — for my own heart urges me strongly. There is a land encircled by steep mountains, rich in flocks and good for grazing, where Prometheus, son of Iapetus, begat noble Deucalion, who was the first to found cities and build temples for the immortals, and the first to be king over men. The neighboring peoples call it Haemonia. In it lies Iolcus, my city, and many other towns besides, where the very name of the island of Aeaea is unknown. Yet they say that Minyas — Aeolian Minyas from there — once founded a city bordering on the Cadmeans. But why do I tell you all these idle things, and speak of our home and of far-famed Ariadne, the lovely daughter of Minos — that glorious name by which men called that enchanting maiden you ask about? Would that, just as Minos made his peace with Theseus concerning her, so your father might be reconciled with us!"

So he spoke, soothing her with gentle, flattering words. But the most painful anguish stirred her heart, and in her distress she answered him with earnest words:

"No doubt such things are fine in Greece — keeping one's promises. But Aeetes is not the sort of man among men that you describe Minos, husband of Pasiphae, to be; nor am I Ariadne's equal. So speak no more of hospitality. But you — remember me when you reach Iolcus; and I will remember you, despite my parents' wishes. May some rumor reach me from afar, or some bird as messenger, when you have forgotten me; or may swift winds carry me myself across the sea

268

from here to Iolcus to snatch you away like a whirlwind,
so that, holding your shame before your eyes,
I might remind you of how you fled by my will. Would that I had been
unexpectedly your hearthmate in your halls at that time.'

So she spoke, shedding pitiful tears down her cheeks; and he addressed her with a crafty reply:
'Poor woman, let empty winds wander as they will,
and likewise a bird-messenger, since you speak of things in vain.
If you come to those shores and the land of Greece,
you will be honored and respected among women and men alike;
they will revere you almost as a goddess,
because through your counsel the sons of some returned home,
and the brothers and companions and vigorous husbands of others were saved from destruction.
And you will tend our marriage bed in our bridal chamber; nothing shall part us from our love
before death, fated for us both, enfolds us.'

So he spoke; and within her the heart melted at his words,
yet she shuddered to look upon deeds of dread.
Poor wretch — she was not long to refuse
to dwell in Greece. For this was Hera's design,
that Aeaean Medea might come to sacred Iolcus as a curse for Pelias,
leaving behind her native land.

Already the handmaids, watching from a distance,
were growing distressed in silence; and the hour of the day called
for the girl to return home to her mother.
But she gave no thought yet to departing, for her heart
took pleasure equally in his looks and in his honeyed words,
until the son of Aeson, keeping watch, spoke up at last:
'It is time to go, before the light of the sun
sets ahead of us, and some stranger notices everything;
we will meet here again another time, coming back to this place.'

So far had they probed each other with gentle words, and then they parted. Medea went gladly toward her companions and the ship, while she headed back to her handmaidens, who came up together to meet her all at once; yet she took no notice of them as they gathered around. For her spirit was soaring aloft among the clouds. Her feet carried her of their own accord to mount the swift chariot, and with one hand she took the reins, and in the other a richly wrought whip to drive the mules; and they rushed toward the city and back to the palace. When Chalciope, mourning for her sons, inquired after her on her return, Medea in her distraction neither heard any of her words nor was inclined to answer her questions. All night long, Aeetes and the bravest captains of his people were plotting outright treachery against the heroes in his halls, with fierce fury in his heart over the outcome of the hateful contest; nor did he suppose for a moment that any of this had been accomplished without his daughters' knowledge.

He told them of neither the passages of the deep sea nor of the grievous storms, except that Circe must wash away the ruthless blood-guilt of Absyrtus; and he commanded them to pray to the immortal gods that Polydeuces and Castor would guide their course ahead through the Ausonian sea, where they would find Circe, daughter of Perse and of Helios.

So the Argo cried out in the darkness; and the sons of Tyndareus leaped up, and raised their hands to the immortal gods, praying for each thing in turn. But dejection gripped the other Minyan heroes. She sped far forward under sail, and they cast into the innermost stream of the Eridanus, where once Phaethon, half-consumed, struck on the breast by the thunderbolt, fell from the chariot of Helios into the deep waters of the lake; and even now it sends up a heavy steam from his still-smouldering wound. No bird can spread its light wings and fly over that water, but in mid-flight it plunges down, caught by the scorching flame. And all around, the Heliades, the daughters of the Sun, wrapped in tall poplars, wail their pitiful lament; and from their eyes they shed bright drops of amber onto the ground — these drops dry in the sunlight upon the sand, but whenever the dark lake's waters wash the shore before the blowing of the loud wind, then all together they roll down in a flood into the Eridanus as it surges on. The Celts have given out the story that these are the tears of Apollo, son of Leto, which he shed in countless drops when of old he came to the holy race of the Hyperboreans, having left the shining heaven at his father's rebuke, in anger over his son, whom divine Coronis bore to him at the springs of Amyrus in rich Lacereia.

And those things are now counted among the stories told to men. But neither desire for food nor drink came over them, nor did their minds turn to any joy. From there they entered the deep stream of the Rhodanus, which flows into the Eridanus; and where the two meet, the water roared and churned together. Now the Rhodanus rises from the innermost depths of the earth, where are the gates and the foundations of Night, and from there it bursts forth: on one side it pours out upon the shores of Ocean, on another it discharges into the Ionian sea, and on another it sends its current into the Sardinian sea and its boundless gulf, through seven mouths. From that river they drove on into stormy lakes, which stretch out endlessly across the land of the Celts. There they might have met a terrible and shameful doom; for a certain branch channel was carrying them toward a gulf of Ocean, into which, had they sailed without knowing it, they would never have returned alive. But Hera leapt down from heaven and cried out from the Hercynian cliff; and all of them were shaken at once with terror, for a great and dreadful thunder crashed through the sky. They turned back at the goddess's urging, and recognized the route along which their homeward journey lay.

For a long time they made their way to the briny shores by the guidance of Hera, passing unharmed through the countless tribes of the Celts and Ligurians. It had seemed to her that the chambers and all the courts of her house were streaming with blood, and a great flame was consuming the drugs with which she used to bewitch whatever strangers came to her; she herself quenched the red gore with blood, scooping it up in her hands, and her dreadful fear subsided. So when dawn came she was washing her hair and garments bright in the moisture of the sea. And beasts, not resembling the ravening beasts of the wild,

Do not, my lord, hand her over to the Colchians to be taken back to her father. She was led astray when she first gave him the charms to enchant the bulls, and then, as so often happens with us through our failings, she fled to escape her overbearing father's heavy wrath. Therefore, dear friend, do not willingly cause the son of Aeson to become an oath-breaker, nor let the girl's father in his furious anger destroy his own child on your account.
