roams in search of its mate and roars;
and the deep glens tremble beneath its voice far off in the mountains,
and the cattle in the fields shudder in great fear,
as do the herdsmen of oxen; but to his men
the voice of their beloved companion calling them was no fearful sound.
They gathered near him, downcast; and he settled them
close to the anchorage among the women,
and spoke, making known to them everything.

"Listen, friends: for three goddesses appeared to me in my distress, girt with goatskin jerkins from the neck down around their backs and waists, like young girls, and stood close above my head; they drew up my cloak with a light hand, and bade me myself to rise and rouse you all to go; and to pay fitting recompense to their mother for all she endured carrying us long within her womb, whenever Amphitrite shall unyoke the swift-rolling chariot of Poseidon. I cannot fully understand the meaning of this prophecy. They declared themselves to be heroines, guardians and daughters of Libya; and all that we ourselves had previously endured on land and sea, they claimed to know every detail. I could no longer see them in the place around me, but some mist or cloud veiled them as they shone."

So he spoke; and all of them were struck with wonder as they listened. Then the greatest of portents befell the Minyans. From the sea onto the land a monstrous horse leaped forth, huge, with its mane tossing golden in the air; it quickly shook the brine from its limbs and sprang away to run, swift as the wind in its stride. Then Peleus, rejoicing, addressed his gathered companions:

"I declare that the chariot of Poseidon has now already been unyoked by the hands of his dear wife; and I look upon no other as our mother than the ship herself: for she, bearing us within her belly, labors ceaselessly with painful toil. But with unwavering strength and tireless shoulders

lifting it up from the sandy earth within, we will carry it whichever way the swift horse has pressed on ahead with his feet. For he will not plunge beneath the dry land; his tracks will, I hope, show us some recess deep beneath the sea.'

So he spoke, and his plan pleased them all as fitting. This is the tale of the Muses; and I, obedient servant of the Pierides, sing it as I heard it in its full truth — that you, who are by far the mightiest sons of princes, by strength and by valor, through the desert sands of Libya carried the ship on your shoulders, with all that was within her, for twelve days and twelve nights together. Who could tell of the toil and the misery that those men endured with their striving? Truly they were of immortal blood, such was the task they undertook, compelled by necessity. But then, rejoicing greatly, they brought it far forward and set it down from their strong shoulders at the waters of Lake Tritonis.

Then, rushing about like mad dogs, they searched for a spring; for upon the parched ground lay thirst along with suffering and pain. But they did not wander in vain; they reached the sacred place where, until just the day before, Ladon, the earth-born serpent, had guarded the all-golden apples in the garden of Atlas, while the Hesperid nymphs busied themselves about him, singing their lovely song. But by then, struck down by Heracles, he lay fallen against the apple-tree trunk; only the tip of his tail still twitched; from his head down to his dark spine he lay lifeless; and where the bitter bile of the Lernaean Hydra had been left in the blood from the arrows, flies were drying themselves on his festering wounds. Nearby, the Hesperides, their hands raised over their heads,

APOLLONIUS RHODIUS

...the silvery ones moaned shrilly among the golden ones; and suddenly the others came rushing together all at once; and the dust and the earth, as they pressed on in haste, came to be right there. Orpheus perceived the divine wonders, and sought to soothe them with his prayers:

"O fair and kindly Spirits, queens, be gracious — whether you are numbered among the heavenly goddesses, or those beneath the earth, or whether you are called solitary nymphs: come, O nymphs, sacred race of Ocean, appear before us and show us, appearing plainly, either some rocky outflow of water, or some sacred stream gushing from the earth, O goddesses, by which we may relieve our burning, unceasing thirst. And if ever again we reach the Achaean land by our seafaring, then shall we bring countless gifts, foremost among the offerings to the goddesses, and libations and feasts, in good will."

So he spoke, pleading with a throbbing voice; and they took pity on them in their distress close by. And first of all they caused grass to spring up from the earth; and above the grass tall shoots burst forth; and then flourishing saplings grew upright high above the ground. Hespere became a poplar, Erytheis an elm; and Aegle became the sacred trunk of a willow tree. And from those trees, just as they had been, they appeared again in that same fixed form — a wondrous marvel — and Aegle addressed the men in need with gentle words:

"Truly, a great boon in all respects has come here to aid your toils — the most shameless one, who robbed the guardian serpent of its life and took the all-golden apples of the goddesses and departed; and a bitter grief has been left to us. For yesterday there came a man most terrible in his violence,

399

and his body; his eyes gleamed fiercely beneath his grim brow; he was merciless; and around him was spread the raw, untanned hide of a monstrous lion; he carried a stout olive-wood club, and with his arrows had slain that monster.
He too had come, as one traveling on foot across the land, parched with thirst; and he ranged through this region searching for water, which he was unlikely to find anywhere. But there was a certain rock near the Tritonian lake; acting on his own impulse, or perhaps by a god's prompting, he struck it below with his heel, and a great rush of water gushed forth; then, pressing both hands and chest to the ground, he drank deeply from the cleft rock, sprawling like a grazing animal, until he had filled his belly to satisfaction.'

So she spoke; and they ran at once with joy to the welcome spring that Aigle had shown them, until they reached it. As when earth-burrowing ants swarm in a crowd around a narrow crevice, or as when flies press eagerly and thickly around a small drop of sweet honey — so then did the Minyans crowd together around the rocky spring. And someone, his lips still wet, spoke with gladness:

'Truly, Heracles has saved his companions even in his absence, worn out as they were with thirst. But if only we might somehow find him as we travel onward across the continent.'

So he spoke; and as they exchanged words, those appointed for this task went off in different directions, each leaping forth to search. For his tracks had been obliterated by the nightly winds —

of the shifting sand. The two sons of Boreas rushed forth, trusting in their wings; and Euphemus trusted in his swift feet, and Lynceus in casting his keen gaze far into the distance; and fifth among them sped Canthus.

Him the will of the gods and his own courage drove on that same path, so that he might learn clearly concerning Heracles — where he had left Polyphemus, son of Eilatus; for he was anxious to inquire on his companion's behalf about all these things. But Polyphemus had founded a famous city among the Mysians and, longing for his return, had gone searching for the Argo far over the mainland; and at last he reached the land of the shore-dwelling Chalybians, where Fate finally overcame him.

And beneath a tall black-poplar a tomb was raised for him, a little way from the sea. But at that moment Lynceus thought he glimpsed Heracles alone, far away in the vast distance, as one sees — or thinks he sees — the new moon dimly through a haze. He came back to his companions and reported that no other searcher could hope to overtake him. The others returned too — swift-footed Euphemus, and the two sons of Thracian Boreas, who had labored in vain.

Canthus — the deadly Fates claimed you in Libya. You had come upon a flock at pasture; a herdsman, defending his sheep while you were taking them to feed your companions in their need, struck you down with a stone — for he was no weakling: he was Caphaurus, grandson of Lycorean Phoebus and of the noble maiden Acacallis, whom once Minos —

A heavy wave of the god carried her away to Libya, his own daughter; and she bore a radiant son to Phoebus, whom they call Amphithemis and Garamas.

Then Amphithemis lay with a Tritonian nymph, and she bore him Nasamon and mighty Caphaurus, who at that time slew Canthos over his own sheep. But Canthos did not escape the harsh hands of the heroes, when they learned what he had done. They carried the body back when they heard of it, the Minyans, and buried him in the earth with laments; and they drove the flocks along with them.

There too on that same day pitiless fate seized Mopsus, son of Ampyx; he did not escape his bitter doom through his prophetic art, for there is no turning aside of death. A terrible serpent lay on the sand, avoiding the midday heat, sluggish of its own accord to strike an unwilling victim; it would not even spring at one who fled from it. But to whatever living creature among all those that the life-bearing earth nourishes it first implants its dark venom, not so much as a cubit is the journey to Hades — not even if Paeon himself, if it is lawful for me to say it openly, were to apply his medicines, once it has merely grazed with its teeth.

For when Perseus, godlike — his mother called him Eurymedon — flew over Libya carrying the freshly severed head of the Gorgon to the king, all the drops of dark blood that fell to the ground sprouted into that race of serpents. Mopsus stepped on the tip of the creature's spine with the flat of his left foot; and it bit him in the middle —

396

the sinew and the muscle, writhing in the grip of pain,
biting into the flesh, he scored it. But Medea and the other
handmaids fled in terror; he probed the bloody wound
boldly, since no overwhelming agony tormented him.
Wretched man — already a limb-loosening stupor
was stealing through his skin, and thick mist poured down over his eyes.
At once he sank down, his limbs weighed heavy to the ground,
and lay helpless; his comrades gathered around him,
and the hero, son of Aeson, stunned by the cruel disaster.
Not even for a short time, though dying, was he destined
to lie beneath the sun. For the venom was rotting his flesh 1530
from within at once, and the hair slipped off his skin in decay.
Quickly they dug a deep grave with bronze mattocks,
working in haste; they cut their own hair,
men and girls alike, mourning the dead man and his pitiful fate;
three times they marched around him in arms,
then laid him, with proper funeral rites, under a mound of earth.

  But when they boarded the ship, with a south wind ready to blow
them across the sea, and tried to work out routes
for escaping from the Tritonian lake, they had no plan
at all, and drifted helplessly all day long. 1540
As a serpent winds along a crooked path
when the fiercest heat of the sun scorches it,
and twists its head this way and that with a hiss, while its eyes
blaze like sparks of fire in its frenzied state,
until it slips through a crack into the depths of its lair —
so the Argo, searching out the navigable mouth of the lake,
wandered for a long time. Then Orpheus called out
that they should take the great tripod of Apollo off the ship
and set it as a gift of appeasement to the native gods, for their return home.
So they went ashore and set up the sacred gift of Phoebus on the land; 1550

To them one like a vigorous young man came to meet them — Triton of great strength — and lifting a clod of earth, he held it out as a guest-gift to the heroes, and spoke:

'Accept this, friends; for it is not possible to offer a lavish guest-gift to those who come to me here. But if you seek to know the passages of this sea, as men often have need of when traveling in foreign lands, I will tell you. For my father Poseidon has appointed me to be the master of this sea. And I rule over the coastal shore — if indeed you have heard anywhere of Eurypylus, born in Libya that feeds wild beasts.'

So he spoke; and Euphemus gladly stretched out his hands for the clod, and answered him in turn:

'If you have knowledge, hero, of Apis and the Minoan sea, tell us truthfully what we ask. For we have not come here willingly, but driven by heavy storms against the edges of this land, we carried our ship, worn out, through the mainland to this body of the lake, weighed down with toil; and we have no idea by what route the voyage leads to reach the land of Pelops.'

So he spoke; and Triton stretched out his hand and pointed into the distance, crying out, showing them the sea and the deep-mouthed channel of the lake:

'That is the outlet to the open sea, where the depth is darkest and most still; on either side the white breakers gleam and shiver; and in between them lies a narrow passage to drive out through. And beyond, that open sea leads over Crete to the heaven-high land of Pelops; but on the right hand —'

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK IV

Before them stood, in the form of a youth, far-swaying Triton, and he lifted a clod from the earth and offered it as a stranger's gift, and spoke thus:
"Take it, friends, for I have no stranger's gift of great worth here with me now to place in the hands of those who beseech me. But if you are searching for a passage through this sea, as is often the need of men passing through a strange land, I will declare it. For my father Poseidon has made me well versed in this sea. And I rule the shore — if perhaps in your distant land you have ever heard of Eurypylus, born in Libya, the home of wild beasts."
Thus he spoke, and readily Euphemus held out his hands toward the clod, and addressed him in reply:
"If perhaps, hero, you know anything of Apis and the sea of Minos, tell us truly, we who ask it of you. For it was not by our own will that we came here, but by the force of heavy storms that we touched the borders of this land, and have carried our ship on our shoulders over the mainland to the waters of this lake, grievously burdened; and we do not know where a passage shows itself for our course to the land of Pelops."
So he spoke; and Triton stretched out his hand and showed them, far off, the sea and the lake's deep mouth, and then addressed them: "That is the outlet to the sea, where the deep water lies still and dark; on each side roll white breakers with shining crests; and the way out between them is narrow. And that sea stretches away in mist to the divine land of Pelops beyond Crete;

1 An old name of the Peloponnesus.

of the right hand, when from the lake you cast into the swell of the sea, keep rowing along the shore while it stretches upward; but when it bends away to the other side toward the land, then a safe voyage is laid out for you, going straight from the jutting headland. But go in gladness, and let no weariness of toil arise from laboring with limbs still in the flower of youth.'

So he spoke in kindness; and they at once stepped aboard the ship, eager to row their way out of the lake. Meanwhile Triton lifted the great tripod and appeared to enter the lake; but after that no one saw him, for he vanished, tripod and all, close at hand. Their hearts were warmed, since one of the blessed gods had met them favorably. And they urged the son of Aeson to choose the finest of the sheep and offer it with prayers. Swiftly he selected one and, lifting it, he cut its throat over the stern, and spoke these words of prayer:

'Divinity, whoever you are who appeared at the edge of this lake — whether you be Triton, great wonder of the sea, or Phorcys, or one whom the Nereids, daughters of the sea, call Nereus — be gracious, and grant us a joyful end to our homeward voyage.'

So he spoke, and together with his prayers slashed the creature's throat and cast it into the water from the stern. And the god rose from the deep, appearing as he truly was to be seen. As when a man fits a swift horse to the wide ring of the racecourse, grasping the willing mane of its shaggy neck, and runs alongside it, while the horse rears proudly at its neck and follows, and the glistening bit in its mouth

On either side they clash against each other with snapping bites. Just as he, gripping the hull of the hollow Argo, drove her forward toward the sea; and his body, from the crown of his head, along his back and flanks down to his belly, showed a form wondrously like that of the blessed gods; but below his hips on either side the tail of the sea-creature stretched out, forking here and there; and with its spines he struck the surface of the water, spines that below divided like the curved horns of the moon. So long he guided her, until he sped her on her way into the open sea as she moved forward; then he dived swiftly into the great deep. The heroes cried out in amazement, seeing that dreadful portent with their own eyes.

There to this day stand the harbor of the Argo, and memorials of the ship, and altars to Poseidon and to Triton; for they halted there that day. Then at dawn, spreading their sails and keeping the desert land on their right, they sped on with the breath of the west wind. At early morning they saw a headland and beyond it an inlet of the sea lying behind the projecting cape. Straightway the west wind fell, and there came a breeze from the gleaming south wind; and their hearts rejoiced at the sound of it. When the sun had set and the evening star rose, that star which brings rest to weary plowmen, then at last, as the wind died away in the dark night, they furled their sails and lowered their tall mast and rowed on with well-polished oars through the whole night and through the day, and through another night that came again. Rocky Carpathus received them from afar, and from there they were about to cross to Crete, which surpasses all other islands in the sea.

But bronze Talos, breaking rocks from a mighty cliff,
prevented them from making fast their cables on shore
as they came down to the Dictaean anchorage. 1640
He remained, last of the bronze race of men sprung from
ash-trees, among the demigods; the son of Cronos had given him
to Europa to be the guardian of the island,
pacing on his bronze feet around Crete three times a day.
Now the rest of his body and his limbs were forged
of bronze and unbreakable; but beneath the sinew at his ankle
ran a blood-filled vein, and over it
a thin membrane held the boundaries of life and death.
The crew, utterly overcome with distress, quickly backed
their ship away from land with their oars. 1650
And they would have been borne wretchedly far from Crete,
suffering alike from thirst and anguish,
had not Medea spoken to them in their despair:
'Listen to me. I alone think I can overcome
this man, whoever he may be, even if his whole body is of bronze,
unless his allotted span of life is without end.
But hold the ship here willingly, out of range
of the rocks, until he yields to being subdued by me.'
So she spoke; and they drew the ship back out of range of the missiles,
resting on their oars, waiting to see what plan she would devise 1660
beyond all expectation. She, holding the folds of her purple
robe up to shade both her cheeks,
stepped up onto the deck; and Jason, taking her hand in his,
guided her as she made her way along the gangways.
There she propitiated the Fates with her songs, and she sang to the Keres,
the soul-devouring, swift hounds of Hades, who wheel about

...whirling through the air are carried over the living.
Kneeling before them she called upon them three times with songs,
and three times with prayers; and setting her mind to malice, with hostile
eyes she cast an evil spell upon the bronze Talos,
and launched against him baneful phantom-shapes in her bitter rage,
beguiling his wits with the dark power of her craft.

O father Zeus, great wonder rises in my heart,
that destruction comes to us not only through disease and wounds —
even one who stands at a distance can bring us harm.
So he, though bronze, was overcome and brought to ruin
by the power of Medea, mistress of many drugs. As he was heaving
heavy boulders to keep them from reaching the harbor,
he grazed his ankle on a sharp crag; and from it
the ichor ran out like molten lead; and he stood no longer
for long upon the jutting headland.
But as some great pine high in the mountains,
which woodcutters have left half-hewn with their keen axes
and gone down from the forest — at night
it first sways in the gusts, but then at last
is wrenched from its base and crashes down —
so he for a time swayed on his tireless feet,
but then at last fell with a tremendous, measureless crash.

That night the heroes made their camp in Crete;
and after that, as the new dawn was shining, they established
a sacred shrine to Athena of Minoa,
drew fresh water and embarked, so that their oars
might drive them first of all past the headland of Salmonis.

But as they sped over the great sea of Crete,
night came upon them in terror — the night men call
the Pall of Darkness; not a star pierced that deadly night,
nor any gleam of the moon; black chaos fell from the sky, or some other
408

The darkness of night rose up from the deep hollows below. The men themselves did not know at all whether they were being carried toward Hades or toward the waters; in their helplessness they left their homeward voyage to the sea, wherever it might bear them. But Jason, raising his hands, cried out with a great voice to Phoebus, calling on him to save them; tears streamed down his troubled cheeks; and he vowed many offerings to Pytho, many to Amyclae, and many boundless gifts to bring to Ortygia.

O son of Leto, you swiftly heard them and came down from heaven to the Melantian rocks that stand in the sea; then, leaping onto one of the two, you held up your golden bow high in your right hand, and the bowstring blazed a dazzling radiance all around. Then a small island of the Sporades came into their sight — opposite the little isle of Hippuris — where they cast their anchor-stones and held fast. And at once the rising dawn shed its light; so they made a sacred precinct and a shaded altar for Apollo in a shady grove, calling on Phoebus as Aegletes, for the sake of his brilliant radiance; and they named that bare island Anaphe, since Phoebus had revealed it to them in their distress. They offered whatever men might prepare to sacrifice on a desolate shore; but when the Phaeacian handmaidens of Medea saw them pouring water onto the burning firebrands, they could no longer hold back laughter in their breasts, since they had always been accustomed to seeing lavish cattle-slaughters in Alcinous' halls. The heroes pelted them back with mocking, shameful words in good-humored jest; and among them there kindled a sweet

...mockery and bitter quarreling. From that song it is that the women of the heroes' island wrangle with their men whenever they propitiate Apollo Aegletes, the guardian of Anaphe, with sacrificial offerings.

But when from there too they had loosed the cables under clear skies, Euphemus then recalled a dream of the night, honoring the glorious son of Maia. For it seemed to him that a divine clod held against his chest in the hollow of his hand was being watered by white drops of milk, and from the clod, small though it was, a woman grew, like a maiden; and he lay with her, overcome by irresistible desire; and he lamented as though he had coupled with a girl whom he himself had nursed at his breast. But she comforted him with gentle words:
"I am of the race of Triton, nurse of your children, dear friend, no maiden; Triton and Libya are my parents. But entrust me to the keeping of Nereus's daughters to dwell in the sea near Anaphe; and I shall come again into the light of the sun hereafter, ready for your descendants."

He then brought the dream to mind and told it to the son of Aeson. Jason pondered the oracles of Apollo in his heart, then spoke up:
"Friend, a great and splendid glory has fallen to your lot. For the gods will make the clod, cast into the sea, into an island, where the younger sons of your sons shall dwell; since Triton gave you this gift of hospitality from the Libyan mainland — it was none other of the immortals but he who met you and gave it."

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK IV

them. And from that sport of the heroes, the women fling such mockery at the men on that island whenever they honor Apollo with sacrifices — Apollo the gleaming god, guardian of Anaphe.
But when they had cast off the mooring lines for the third time in calm weather, Euphemus recalled a dream of the night, in which he had honored the glorious son of Maia. For it seemed to him that the god-given clod of earth he held in his palm against his chest was being nursed by white streams of milk, and that from it, small as it was, a woman grew like a virgin; and he, overcome by strong desire, lay with her in a lover's embrace; and even as he united with her he felt pity for her, as though she were a young girl whom he himself had been nursing at his own breast; but she comforted him with gentle words:
"I am the daughter of Triton, dear friend, and the nurse of your children — no maiden; Triton and Libya are my parents. But return me to the daughters of Nereus, to live in the sea near Anaphe; I shall rise again into the light of the sun, to prepare a home for your descendants."
He stored this memory carefully in his heart and reported it to Aeson's son; and Jason pondered a prophecy of the Far-Shooter and spoke up:
"My friend, great and glorious renown has come to you. For when you cast this clod into the sea, the gods will make it an island, where your children's children shall live; for Triton gave it to you as a gift of hospitality from the Libyan mainland. No other immortal gave it to you but he, when he met you."

413

So he spoke; and Euphemus did not make vain the response of the son of Aeson. Gladdened by the divine prophecy, he cast the clod beneath the sea. From it rose up the island of Calliste, sacred nurse of the descendants of Euphemus, who once had dwelt in Sintian Lemnos, and being driven from Lemnos by Tyrrhenian men had come as suppliants to Sparta; and from Sparta the noble son of Autesion, Theras, led them to the island of Calliste, and changed its name to Thera after himself. But these things came to pass after the time of Euphemus.

From there, swiftly crossing the vast swell of the sea, they put in at the shores of Aegina; and straightaway they fell to a blameless contest about the water, as to who could draw it and reach the ship first. For both need and a great wind pressed them. Even now the young men of the Myrmidons still compete in that race, carrying full water-jars on their shoulders, running swiftly on their feet for the prize of victory.

Be gracious, O race of blessed heroes! And may these songs grow sweeter year by year for mankind to sing. For now I have come to the glorious end of your toils; since no further trial befell you on your return from Aegina, nor did any blasts of wind hinder you; but calmly, passing by the land of Cecrops and Aulis, and the cities of Opuntian Locris within Euboea, you gladly set foot on the shores of Pagasae.

THE ARGONAUTICA, BOOK IV

So he spoke; and Euphemus did not let the prophecy go unfulfilled but, encouraged by it, cast the clod into the depths. From it rose an island, Calliste, the sacred nurse of the sons of Euphemus, who in earlier times had lived in Sintian Lemnos, and from Lemnos were driven out by Tyrrhenians and came to Sparta as refugees; and when they left Sparta, Theras, the noble son of Autesion, led them to the island Calliste, and from himself he gave it the name Thera. But all this happened after the time of Euphemus.
Then they steadily left behind long stretches of sea and put in at the beach of Aegina; and there at once they competed in a harmless contest over who would draw water first and carry it back to the ship. Both their need and a relentless wind drove them on. Even to this day the young men of the Myrmidons take up full-brimming jars on their shoulders and race swiftly to win.
Be gracious, race of blessed heroes! And may these songs grow sweeter year after year to sing among men. For now I have reached the glorious end of your labors; for no misfortune overtook you on your way home from Aegina, and no storm of winds stood against you; but quietly you skirted the Cecropian land and Aulis inside Euboea and the Opuntian cities of the Locrians, and gladly stepped ashore upon the beach of Pagasae.
